speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: Our universities and academic institutions are places of higher learning, research and innovation.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: They are also workplaces where faculty members, researchers and students spend a significant amount of their time.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: In recent years the academic work environment has become increasingly stressful, leading to the rising incidence and prevalence of mental health issues among university researchers and graduate students.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: There may be several reasons why mental health issues are becoming prevalent in academia.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: One of the biggest causes arguably is the constant pressure to perform.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: The academic path can be both long and narrow.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: It may also come with significant opportunity costs.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: Having committed typically around 10 to 15 of the most productive years in their 20s and 30s to acquiring an increasingly specialised skill set as an early career researcher, the scope for an alternative career tends to get increasingly narrower as they progress in their training as graduate student, postdoctoral researcher and then junior professor.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: The pressure to continue down this path and succeed as a tenured academic can be enormous.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: Additionally, the nature of academic research for some disciplines can be arduous and unpredictable.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: The demands of laboratory experiments or field surveys typically require individuals to work after hours and over weekends.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: These long, irregular and gruelling hours of research inevitably compromise work-life balance and can have significant impacts on the mental health of early career researchers.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: Many of them are also at an age when they are trying to start a family, and so these mental health impacts may extend to their partners and other loved ones as well.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: Furthermore, many research-intensive universities now consider various publication related metrics when evaluating the performance of their faculty members and researchers.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: This can create a "publish or perish" mentality which in turn creates immense pressures, especially among early career researchers to publish quickly, frequently and in the most highly regarded scientific journals.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: A strong publication track record is critical for securing a good post-doctoral position and academic tenure.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: However, the overwhelming and constant pressure to publish can lead to persistent feelings of anxiety, resulting in burnouts and other mental health issues.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: Another major contributor to mental health issues among early career researchers is job insecurity.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: Many individuals who embark on an academic career may aspire to be a tenured professor someday.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: But there are just not enough professor positions for the growing number of PhD graduates to fill.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: As a result, many early career researchers are on short-term contracts supported by research grants.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: The duration and size of these grants can be variable and unpredictable, leading to uncertainties for long-term employment.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: This lack of job security can also lead to persistent stress and anxiety as researchers constantly worry about their next contract and future career prospects.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: The constant cost of living concerns can lead to a vicious cycle of poor mental health and decreased academic performance, with individuals struggling to cope with the rigorous demands of academic life as graduate students while also managing their challenging financial situation as young adults.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: Indeed, there may be a common but misguided perception in academia that admitting to struggling with one's mental health is somehow a sign of weakness, incompetence or inadequacy.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: This stigma can lead individuals to feel like they need to hide their struggles to fit in or to maintain their academic standing among their peers.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: Left unchallenged, this stigma can cause individuals to delay seeking help or treatment for mental health concerns, which can lead to a worsening of symptoms and other detrimental impacts on their personal and academic life.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: To address the growing mental health issues facing the academic community, we may wish to consider the following suggestions, some of which are already being implemented in our local universities and research institutions, but we can always do more.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: First, we could invest more in mental health research to contextualise and better understand the extent and nature of the mental health problem within Singapore's academic community.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: This may help us develop more effective and bespoke solutions.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: Second, we could provide more mental health support services, including workshops, support groups and mental health professionals to create an ecosystem of affordable and accessible mental health resources on campus for those in need.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: Third, we could make greater efforts to raise awareness and reduce the stigma associated with mental health in academia.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: Importantly, we could create a culture of openness and support by providing training for senior faculty and staff on how to identify and support individuals who may be struggling.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: By doing so, we can destigmatise and normalise our discussions on mental health.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: This may include providing more opportunities for remote work and flexible schedules and creating policies that limit after-work emails and meetings.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: Its main goals are to destigmatise mental health conditions in the NUS community and support those who seek help.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: It provides free and confidential mental well-being check-ins, emotional support sessions and a 24-hour hotline, among other services.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: I declare that I am an NUS professor.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: Of course, other universities in Singapore provide similar initiatives and support to their academic communities as well.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: The quality of our universities and research institutions plays a critical role in maintaining this status.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: More importantly, a physically and mentally healthy research workforce, which includes graduate students and researchers at all levels, is needed to ensure the consistent production of top-quality research in Singapore.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: Furthermore, the academic community in Singapore is diverse and international, with individuals from different cultures, backgrounds and experiences working together towards the common goal of creating impactful, new knowledge, science and technologies.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: Providing a supportive and inclusive environment that promotes the mental well-being of all members of our academic community will enable us to attract and retain top talents from around the world and maintain Singapore's role as a global knowledge and innovation hub.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: Addressing mental health in academia is not just a moral imperative but also an economic one.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: By investing in mental health initiatives in academia, we can improve the productivity and performance of our academic workforce, which can have a positive impact on our economy as a whole.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: Let us work together to create a culture of openness, support and understanding in the academic community, where individuals can seek help without fear of stigma or judgement and realise their full potential.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In most countries, the nature of healthcare provision is highly contested and debated because of its critical importance.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In many countries, including our own, healthcare is also a vital sector for the economy, creating many jobs directly and indirectly.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: It is this single theme that my speech will address today.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In my speech, which supports the Motion, I will talk about: (a) addressing recruitment and retention among healthcare workers; (b) raising the productivity of healthcare workers; and (c) improving the outcomes from the healthcare system as a whole without increasing cost proportionately by addressing sources of health problems upstream and by other means.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Before I proceed, I declare my interest as the chairman of a company that does consulting work in the healthcare space, among other verticals.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Without a micro-second's hesitation, my daughter said, and I quote, "Give them decent working hours, respect at work and good pay." Indeed, this is a major long-term challenge we face.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: We can build the wards and clinics, we can buy the equipment, but how can we attract and retain workers in the sector such that churn is minimised, such that there is a core of professionals from whom future leaders can be drawn, such that there is a good learning curve, a sufficient accumulation of experience and skills to elevate service and effectiveness so as to ensure good outcomes for patients?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: There are media and anecdotal reports of facilities that are unused due to a lack of manpower.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: For example, a recent report from TODAY, citing a private doctor, said, "As a matter of fact, several private hospitals have closed some hospital wards and operating theatres due to a shortage of nurses.” The all-important manpower challenge in healthcare unpacks itself into a few bundles of issues – compensation, working hours, working conditions and career laddering, and productivity and, also, as part of that, that should address ensuring that the work feels meaningful.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Junior doctors' pay was increased as well recently but, as per the reply to my recent Parliamentary Question (PQ) on this, the 7% to 13% starting salary increase applies to house officers and first-year medical officers (MOs).

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: However, more experienced junior doctors, namely, eligible in-service MOs or residents up to postgraduate Year 6 and dental officers up to postgraduate Year 4, could expect a salary adjustment based on their years in service and bond period rather than an across-the-board increase, as I understand it.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Clearly, to attract and retain talent, compensation has to be competitive.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Moreover, in healthcare, talent can migrate across national borders.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Many countries are short of experienced healthcare staff.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I am aware of academic studies that are occasionally published to this effect but I am not aware that there is a regular Government publication to this effect.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Next, Sir, on managing working hours and burnout.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: There is no point raising pay if there is under-capacity and working hours rise after that such that pay per hour remains the same or actually falls.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: There is evidence that the same training outcomes can be obtained with a cap of 70 hours per week versus 80, as I explained in my previous Committee of Supply speech.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: This would also require systems to be streamlined so that junior doctors and, indeed, nurses, spend more time on patient care and training rather than administrative tasks.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I would also repeat my calls to move towards 100% compliance with the current 10-hour intervals between duty periods and after in-house calls, up from 90% now, ensuring no under-reporting of hours and taking concrete steps to shorten the time spent on handing over administrative and peripheral duties.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I understand that conditions for junior doctors are being reviewed in the public healthcare system now.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I hope that the need to optimise working hours will be fully considered in that process.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Workload is, of course, a function of healthcare demand vs manpower capacity.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Healthcare demand will rise steadily as our population ages and, indeed, we are one of the fastest-ageing populations in the world.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: This should help with meeting demand if nurses stay in the profession.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Right now, the proportion of Singaporeans among enrolled nurses is a little over 60%.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I wonder if this number is sufficient to meet the needs of the future to generate enough of a pipeline of nurses for future senior nurse practitioner, mentoring and leadership roles.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Does the Ministry review the number of nursing scholarships given with this in mind?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Do such reviews extend to the awarding of a sufficient number of postgraduate scholarships in nursing, given the increasing complexity and technology dependence in the healthcare sector going forward?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Currently there appears to be only one academic programme which provides a Masters in Nursing requirement for advanced practice nurses.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: So as to strengthen the Singapore Core in professions like nursing, we should provide preferential consideration to foreigners who are in these professions who have lived and worked here for some time and have demonstrated a capacity to integrate well into our society to obtain permanent residency and, eventually, citizenship.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I believe some other Members of this House have called for this before and the Government has said it is open to such an idea.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: To add on to this, I would repeat my call for the giving of citizenship to be made more transparent, with the availability, for example, of an online points-based calculator, similar to what you see in some other countries.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: This may make Singapore more attractive to healthcare professionals from other countries by providing more clarity and assurance.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Next, Mr Deputy Speaker, Sir, on the role of pharmacists.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: This is already being considered in Australia, though there has been some pushback associated with this.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Our pharmacists already make adjustments to dosing of drugs for some chronic medications, and advanced practice nurses also have cooperative prescribing models in our local healthcare institutions.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: This may negatively impact general practitioners (GPs) initially but I have some suggestions relating to GPs which I will come to in a minute.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Next, Mr Deputy Speaker, Sir, I would like to touch on the necessary role of other allied healthcare professionals and medical personnel.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I note that the Government has plans for a greater role for community pharmacists in promoting things like health screening and vaccinations.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I spoke about the vital role of both health screening and vaccinations in my Adjournment Motion on preventive healthcare last year as well as via PQs previously.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: MRNA technology is already spawning potentially revolutionary developments in medicine that could lead to radical breakthroughs in decades to come.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: But turning back to current realities, it would seem that we are lagging behind many developed countries in terms of the more routine types of vaccination, like influenza vaccines.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: This can limit the incidence of chronic or catastrophic conditions further downstream.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: There are plans to raise the number of allied healthcare professionals.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Such professionals can play a critical role in community healthcare, nudging healthier lifestyles and appropriate help-seeking behaviours, including for mental health conditions, as well as helping those with chronic conditions prevent the development of complications.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In the Serangoon ward of Aljunied Group Representation Constituency (GRC), my volunteers and I have had the honour of working with Tan Tock Seng Hospital (TTSH) Community Partners to conduct a health talk and consultation session at a rental block.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: We also refer cases we come across to TTSH Community Partners, or TTSH CP, which also stations nurses at the Community Care Services Singapore facility at Golden Ginger in Serangoon North at certain times, to make some screening and advice available to the people who live in the area.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: These are commendable and beneficial interventions, and I hope that these can be replicated in other areas that currently lack this.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: These should eventually be funded centrally as they do not require costly infrastructure and could also allow local nurses, physiotherapists, occupational therapists and podiatrists with families to, perhaps, work part-time near their homes in their own communities.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The model for deployment of such allied healthcare professionals is often to leverage events that attract people to consider health issues.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: However, some evidence from a survey conducted by Lifebuoy suggests that most Singaporeans take a rather passive approach to their own health and do not often or always proactively seek out information on how to improve their health.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Hence, it behooves us to find methods that are more in line with what, in business marketing, is referred to as "hunting", that is, direct sales, as opposed to "farming", or attracting people to come to you.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: These are areas of high footfall, particularly among older people, who may benefit more from healthcare interventions.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: It may be helpful if personnel who are fluent in vernacular languages can approach them in these settings, in a more proactive way, to promote ideas, such as vaccination and health screening, or even to perform certain basic screening activities on the spot.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: For younger demographic segments, what might work better are, perhaps, strategies that rely on social media.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Next, Mr Deputy Speaker, Sir, let me move on to the role of GPs.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Our roughly 1,800 GP clinics play an important role in our healthcare system as the first line of defence for non-emergencies.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: This role is set to increase with the advent of Healthier SG.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: When we speak of attracting and retaining good healthcare professionals in our system, we should not neglect our GPs.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: If there are too many exits from the GP sector, this may dent our ability to achieve our primary healthcare and Healthier SG goals.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Also, a study of primary healthcare quality by the National Healthcare Group published in the journal "Asia Pacific Family Medicine" in 2014, which polled 85 experts, concluded that Singapore's system suffers from several issues, and I quote: "The primary care system in Singapore received an average of 10.9 out of 30 possible points...

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Singapore was categorised as a 'low' primary care country according to the experts." The earnings of primary care physicians, compared to specialists, were one of several factors cited.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In my opinion, most of our GPs are thoughtful and well-informed individuals, who should have good ideas for constructive policy change.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The Ministry of Health (MOH) does Primary Care Surveys every 10 years or so to determine, primarily, the economic parameters around the primary care sector, but much more can be done.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Right now, drug sales representatives often sell drugs to individual GPs.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: And this means fragmentation and far less bargaining power and economies of scale.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: As an aside, I was once queuing to see a GP and someone behind me in the queue got in to see the GP before me.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I did not mind, but I was just curious.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: So, I went up to the receptionist and I asked the receptionist why this happened and she said she had deprioritised me as I was wearing a tie at the time and she thought I was a drug sales rep rather than a patient.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Lastly, would the Government, as part of the surveying effort I referred to earlier, identify GPs who have spare capacity – meaning that there are certain times of day when they do not see so many patients – and find ways to engage such GPs to augment the capacity in polyclinics or other public healthcare institutions, if they are keen to do so?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Anecdotally, it seems that the density of GP networks has seen some long-term increase and competition has risen.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: One effect of this may be that some GPs – not all – have some spare capacity at certain times of the day, on certain days.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I am reminded of an amusing conversation I had once as a young Economic Development Board (EDB) officer.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: One of my colleagues was talking to another manager.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The manager said that he could not increase output without a commensurate increase in headcount, to which, the first person said, "Ah, yes, but that assumes zero productivity growth." I have never forgotten this little bit of wisdom, so pithily conveyed.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Of course, as healthcare demand grows, we will need to hire more staff.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: But we need to manage the rate of that increase so as to manage cost, as well as to manage population pressures that may arise from excessive inflows of foreign manpower – and I use the term "manpower" here in a gender-neutral way, of course.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: There are advances in healthcare technology to draw upon and best practices available worldwide.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: For example, telemedicine can enhance staff utilisation and save time for patients as well.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Some survey evidence suggests that Singaporeans are open to virtual consultations.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: For example, service robots could perform some of the functions of a healthcare concierge.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Robotics devices can also play a role in rehabilitative medicine.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I am aware that some of these innovations have come to our healthcare system and more are being considered.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I am also aware that this is not a new topic.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In 2012, MOH launched the Healthcare Productivity Roadmap and, in 2017, MOH announced the Healthcare Productivity Fund.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: There are also the National Healthcare Productivity and Innovation Awards.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: My suggestion here is that the Government measure healthcare labour productivity from time to time and publish the results, benchmarked against productivity standards in other global cities.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I think it would be useful to make city-by-city comparisons in this regard.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: There would be various types of metrics that could be considered.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Ideally, we should measure public and private healthcare separately for the sake of comparison.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: And this data could be used to identify good outliers, where best practices and case studies can be documented and shared.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: If we do not know where we are at, we cannot get to where we want to go.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Some experts speak of a youth mental health crisis, a phenomenon which may not be unique to Singapore by any means.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: For example, a Boston-based company called "OM1" recently built an AI platform called "PHenOM" to help psychiatrists enhance their diagnostic and treatment effectiveness and efficiency.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Holmusk's mental health analytics platform is of a large scale.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: We need to grasp the opportunities to meet those challenges.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: And this will have to be done by our healthcare professionals, the people who must be at the heart of all we do in healthcare, for, without them, nothing is possible.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: At the end of the day, healthcare is, and will remain, must remain, a profoundly human endeavour.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: There is no more important goal in healthcare than attracting, retaining and bringing out the best from our great healthcare workers.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: And before I conclude, Mr Deputy Speaker, Sir, I would just like to join my hon friend Mr Gerald Giam and other hon Members of the House in expressing our whole society's profound gratitude to our wonderful nurses, and to wish them in advance a very happy Nurses' Day to come.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Despite the tremendous increase in demand for medical services, they have continued to provide exceptional care with professionalism and empathy.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: We are truly indebted to our healthcare workers and administrators for their tireless efforts throughout this challenging period.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Your courage and resilience have made a tremendous impact in our fight against the pandemic, and I would like to express my deepest gratitude for your incredible work.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: The contributions of our healthcare professionals should not, however, only just be recognised during times of crisis.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: We should still recognise their invaluable contributions moving forward, as we work towards living in a world with COVID-19, post-COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: It is easy to overlook the exceptional healthcare system in Singapore and fail to appreciate the dedication and hard work that go into providing top-notch healthcare services across the country.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: And we should continue to uphold this, not because we want to remain competitive globally, but because it is the responsible thing to do for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Good health is essential for individuals to lead productive and fulfilling lives, and access to quality healthcare is crucial for maintaining good health.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: And because healthcare impacts everyone, I was happy to see this Motion tabled.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: I fully agree with the hon Members that we should take a whole-of-Government approach to healthcare.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: This is critical because it recognises that healthcare is not just the responsibility of the healthcare sector, but also involves many other sectors and factors.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: By taking a comprehensive approach, Singapore can identify and address the root causes of healthcare issues and improve health outcomes for its citizens.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: I want to speak on the following four points which I believe should be given more attention.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: First, on accessibility of healthcare services for the elderly and persons with disabilities.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Singapore's population is ageing and the demand for geriatric services looks to increase.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: As our population ages, it becomes more disposed to chronic medical conditions, cognitive impairments, falls, frailty which can significantly impact the quality of life.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: This calls for specialised knowledge about the ageing process and the optimal management of multiple medical conditions, medications and physical impairments.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Teaching Singaporeans how to age is something which should be invested in as well, and a holistic approach is required, prioritising not just diagnosis and treatment but also functional ability, social interaction and psychological well-being.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Courses, such as arts, nutrition and digital literacy, exist.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: However, I believe more can be done to provide more physical and mental well-being courses.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: With an increasing Singaporean population of elderly individuals, the importance of gerontology cannot be understated, as it enables our silver generation to maintain independence, improve outcomes and live fulfilling lives.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Unfortunately, PwDs often face barriers to accessing healthcare, including physical, communication and attitudinal barriers.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: In addition to physical accessibility, healthcare providers can also improve their attitudes towards PwDs by providing education and training for their staff.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: They can also work towards promoting disability inclusion in healthcare policies and procedures.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Currently, there are many small- and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) and Non-Governmental Organisation (NGOs) that are in the space of enabling PwDs and it would be good to have more dialogues on continual improvement of services for PwDs and increasing access and awareness of such services for PwDs.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: By taking these steps, healthcare providers can ensure that PwDs have access to the same quality of healthcare services as those without disabilities.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: It is essential to prioritise accessible and equitable healthcare to better build a healthier and more inclusive society.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: I now move on to my second point, as we celebrate the triumphs of our Team Singapore athletes in Phnom Penh, we should also recognise the hard work and sacrifice our athletes and their entourage have made to bring glory to Singapore.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Our elite athletes often face intense physical and mental pressures.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: These pressures can affect their performance, long-term physical health and overall well-being.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: To excel in their sport, athletes must maintain a rigorous training discipline, adhere to strict dietary requirements and overcome physical injuries.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Unfortunately, these pressures can often lead to mental health problems such as anxiety, depression and eating disorders.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: In addition to physical pressures, many athletes face significant social pressures.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: They may feel pressure from teammates, coaches, fans and the media.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: This can lead to additional mental health problems, including stress, burnout and a lack of self-confidence.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: This can include mental health support, sports psychology and mentoring from experienced athletes.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: It is also essential for athletes to understand that it is okay to prioritise their mental and physical health over their sport.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Many athletes, such as May Ooi and Constance Lien, have recognised this and have become advocates for mental health awareness and self-care.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: By acknowledging the pressures that elite athletes face and providing the necessary support, we can help them perform at their best while maintaining their long-term physical and mental health.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Therefore, I hope that more support can be put into handling these unique needs of our national teams.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Third, on creating a vibrant sports and fitness culture.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: It is true that we often take our health for granted until an event impacts us directly.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Recently, a friend passed away from a heart attack.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: There is a difference between training and exercising.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: We participate in Co-curricular activities (CCA), and sports CCAs teach you how to train – push your physical boundaries for performance, but exercise is about maintenance, mobility and lifestyle.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Exercise should be a habit and a lot to do with forming habits has to do with convenience, routine and accessibility.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Some Members may know that Dr Tan Yia Swam is an avid parkour practitioner.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Parkour, is a sport of jumping, climbing and sliding over and through a terrain.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: In Singapore, this happens to be an urban terrain and I am happy to see that such projects and facilities being built in Somerset and Lakeside.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: I hope more urban-centric sport facilities will be built to match Singapore's landscape and interests.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: I hope and would also like to also encourage programmes to go together with these facilities.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: To do that, instructors need to be trained, qualified and hired.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: But to empower this registry, the trainers need to have updated and relevant content to teach.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: I would encourage SportSG, Health Promotion Board (HPB), MOE and People's Association (PA) to have more discussions about the delivery of relevant, age-appropriate physical programmes that cater to a vibrant, active Singapore population.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Fourth, verbal abuse towards frontliners working tirelessly to keep society functioning during this pandemic is a deplorable issue.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Despite their unwavering commitment to rigorous job demands, healthcare workers, essential workers and other public-facing roles have been subject to verbal abuse, shaming and criticism.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: In addition to it being emotionally draining, verbal abuse can lead to mental and physical health issues and impact the professional and personal lives of those affected.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Therefore, it is crucial to recognise the value of our frontliners and to show support by offering gratitude, recognising their hard work and taking ownership of our collective responsibilities.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Frontliners deserve our fullest respect, support and empathy.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Recognising and addressing this issue is vital in holding those responsible accountable for their actions.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: In addition, public campaigns can educate people on the importance of respecting frontline workers and the consequences of their actions.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: They have worked long hours under challenging conditions while risking their health to care for patients.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: As the pandemic begins to subside, the Government must continue to support medical workers even after the pandemic.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: The pandemic has taken a toll on their mental health and well-being, and they must receive support and resources to deal with any long-term effects.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: This includes providing adequate personal protective equipment, training and vaccination.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Healthcare workers at the forefront of infectious disease outbreaks must be thoroughly protected against any potential hazard they may face in the future.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: By showing support and appreciation for medical workers after the pandemic, we create a sense of value for their role within our society.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Their sacrifice and hard work deserve recognition, and this can go a long way in keeping them motivated and inspired.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: The Government should continue to support medical workers to build a brighter future for our healthcare industry and the patients that rely on them.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: As Members of Parliament, we share the same goal: to create a healthier, more resilient Singapore, for generations to come.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Our nation's healthcare system is an essential part of that objective and I am grateful for the opportunity to engage in a constructive dialogue on this vital issue.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: I want to touch on two broad topics.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: First, and unsurprisingly, on mental health and second, on our efforts in the Malay Community through the "Saham Kesihatan" initiative.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: It is integral not only to an individual's well-being but also to the health and productivity of our society.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: I am glad that Dr Tan Yia Swam brought it up.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: We must acknowledge the challenges posed by Dr Tan Yia Swam head-on and continue to work collaboratively to find effective solutions.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Conversations around mental health have become much easier amongst Singaporeans over the years and this is not a coincidence.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: It is made possible by the efforts from the Government through the Inter-Agency Taskforce on Mental Health and Well-being, private sectors, community partners and ground-up groups to destigmatise mental health issues.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: While we have made strides in terms of awareness on mental health, we must recognise that there is still much to be done, particularly in how we can directly mitigate issues of mental health.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: I want to revisit some of the points raised in my Adjournment Motion back in 2020 to align with Dr Tan Yia Swam.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: During that speech, I shared the acronym "LAST".

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Briefly, "L" for literacy, "A" for accessibility, "S" for screening and "T" for time-outs.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Being an educator, I truly share Dr Tan Yia Swam's sentiment on the importance of education.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: We must continue to raise mental health literacy among our citizens.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: It should be introduced early, starting with our schools.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: The intention is simple, we want to create some normalcy and promote early detection and intervention of mental health issues, leading to better outcomes and quality of life for individuals.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: It would also be helpful to reduce the societal burden of untreated mental health issues and contribute to the overall well-being of our community.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Now, I am confident that we can foster a community that eradicates mental health stigmatisation.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: But I also have to remind myself that such shifts in mindsets will not come easy, will not come instantaneously nor come so soon.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: And like many education programmes, changes can take quite some time.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: As a teacher 20 years ago, I had students who needed special attention in class.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: People questioned me on why I bothered to take such differentiated approach at that time.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Twenty years on, we can observe that people, the society, have become accepting, and thanks to the efforts of both public and private sectors including advocates like Hon Member and Jalan Besar Group Representation Constituency (GRC) colleague, Denise Phua, students now who require special attention in class are now embraced and provided with timely and appropriate intervention.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Although we have not achieved the same level of acceptance for mental health, we must persevere.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: We must continue with a "whole-of-society" approach towards mental health and this means an active participation from the whole-of-Government, private sectors, community partners, ground-up groups and religious organisations.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: As Members of Parliament, we must wholeheartedly believe in this cause and strive to make it a reality.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: I commend the efforts by Members of this house and those before us who have been advocating for mental health.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: When we, as a society, a whole-of-society amplify the voices of those who have experienced mental health issues, we help to break down the barriers that prevent individuals from seeking help and create a more inclusive and supportive environment.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: We want them to access mental health services without fear or stigma, discrimination or barriers such as cost, waiting time, transportation, or even distance.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Due to the lack of resources, people who need help may turn to untrained mental health practitioners or rely on self-help resources, this may not provide the same level of support and expertise as a trained one.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: I want to draw focus on the mental well-being of our healthcare workers.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: The nature of their work is more than just a job; it is a calling that requires deep commitment and dedication.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: We must provide support and resources to help them cope with the stress and challenges inherent in their professions, which will ultimately lead to improved patient care.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Moreover, we must address the harassment and abuse faced by healthcare workers, both physically and online, as it directly impacts their mental well-being.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: We must say, “If you abuse our healthcare workers, there will be consequences”.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: I look forward to the implementation of the measures to protect them.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: (In Malay):   Minister Masagos recently announced that the Malay community has shown progress in several health indicators.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: This includes the number of Malay patients with high blood cholesterol.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: However, we still need to continue efforts to look after our community's health.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: This programme is in line with Healthier SG's goal of making disease prevention a personal commitment.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: We need to take proactive steps to undergo frequent health screenings, adopt an active lifestyle and have a healthy diet.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Besides individual efforts, this whole-of-community initiative can also bring about changes.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: This is where the Healthy Investment Programme by M3@Towns can provide opportunities for physical activities, raise awareness on the importance of maintaining a healthy lifestyle and identify potential risks linked to obesity.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: By working with other agencies such as HPB and Active SG, and as individuals making healthy choices, we can continue to progress and improve the health of our community and reduce the prevalence of obesity and other health-related issues.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: I urge our community to take this opportunity to participate in the activities organised by M3@Towns.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Remember, it is our obligation to stay healthy.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: And if we are healthy, we will be able actively contribute to our family and the development of our community and nation.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: (In English): As we continue the discourse on our healthcare system, it is important to acknowledge that we have a strong foundation and must continue to build on it.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: As individuals, we must recognise the vital role each one of us plays in shaping the fabric of our society.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Each individual in our society serves as a vital cog in this complex machinery of our nation’s well-being.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Every cog, no matter how small or seemingly insignificant, contributes to the smooth operation and overall success of the system.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: And when one individual is down, others must step up to care and help.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: It is only through our collective efforts, with each and everyone of us working in harmony, that we can make a lasting, positive impact on the health landscape of our cherished nation.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Their passion, deep knowledge and unwavering commitment to balance meaningful, insightful discourse throughout their time in Parliament have not gone unnoticed.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Together, we can build a brighter, more resilient and healthier future for all.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Over the past few months, we have debated on Healthier SG and then the White Paper on COVID-19 Response.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Minister Ong has also updated this House on the three strategic pillars of Singapore healthcare going forward – acute care, public health and aged care.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: There were also several Forward SG dialogues giving birth to lots of ideas and initiatives.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: I applaud MOH and the whole-of-Government for the comprehensive holistic approach that is being taken, but we must all recognise that this is a marathon and not a sprint.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: There is a lot to be done and will need whole of Singapore to be committed to act together for a healthier Singapore especially as we mature rather rapidly in age.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Continued dialogue amongst all stakeholders is very important to listen, to clarify, to prioritise issues and to collaborate on solutions as we move forward, will be a key imperative.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: For this debate, I will focus my attention on what the community and the private sector can and ought to do to complement and supplement the whole-of-Government efforts to support our healthcare workforce and our healthcare strategic transformation initiatives.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Inevitably, I will also have policy consideration questions and recommendations which I hope MOH and the whole-of-Government can consider to take on board.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: There sometimes is this unrealistic expectation of “being served” in hospitals.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Asking	to be served water much like what we would do at a restaurant is the wrong expectation.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Overusing of call buttons for minor requests is not being considerate.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: And hurling abuses at anyone, let alone folks who are actually helping us, is absolutely unacceptable.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Instead, a smile, a "please", a "thank you" would go a long way to show some consideration and appreciation.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: I am sure the healthcare staff are trained to be empathetic and sympathetic, which if not so, they should be.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Still, the families and the patients should not think it our right to let go of our anger and frustrations on the healthcare staff, be they doctors, nurses, allied health professionals, support care staff or even the hospital security guards.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Think of one thing we are grateful for.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: And consider the wise age-old golden rule: “Do unto others as you would have them do unto you”.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: That said, still, there will be bad behaviours and I support MOH’s plans to have a concerted, across-the-board policy to handle and address the bad apples amongst us even as I wish and hope that as a community, we can all do better.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Nurses, allied healthcare and care support workers will become increasingly important along with family physicians, doctors and medical specialists, as Singapore heads into becoming a super-aged nation.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: The community ourselves must recognise that we have just as important a role to play.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: The first order of the day is to individually keep an active and healthy lifestyle to prevent chronic illnesses.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Next, the community can help ourselves by forming little support groups among residents or neighbours to support one another.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: These little support groups can be like little satellites receiving and disseminating correct, right healthcare-related information.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: These groups can organise themselves with some governance and help to visit their neighbours and bring those in need for hospital checks, check that they are taking their medication and so on.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: I understand that some of this is already happening but perhaps not in a cohesive, organised way.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: I guess the best example is whatever we managed to rally during COVID-19.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: So, now, in peace times, how do we repeat that?

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Going forward, we can be more coordinated and more collaborative.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Then, the community may organise health screening, community exercises like Zumba, hikes to MacRitchie, Tai Chi and so on.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: The issue is how to get more people involved and keep it sustained.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: In my speech at the Healthier SG debate, I shared about GoodLife!

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Makan at Block 52 Marine Terrace, an initiative of Montfort Care FSC as well as	“Share-a-Pot” at the Caritas	Agape Village in Toa Payoh.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: These and other ground-up initiatives like the SG Mental Well-being Network or the Family of Wisdom by Dementia Singapore or Caring Commuter Champions who assist our public transport commuters who have visual impairment or physical disabilities or may be seniors with dementia, during their daily public transport commute.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: These are examples of what the community can do to be a part of the Singapore healthcare ecosystem.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Serendipity has it that I just attended this morning a heartwarming Sing Out Loud! performance at Esplanade by nine seniors with dementia accompanied by nine Kindergarten 1 and 2 children.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: The seniors are residents of the St Joseph's Home and the children are preschoolers attending the childcare centre which is located in the same compound as the St Joseph's Home Infant and Childcare Centre.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: It will be remiss of me not to mention the Convent Yuki and the flourishing fund initiatives sprouted out when friends transitioned into the second half of their retirement and supported seniors like my mother-in-law Mrs Lily Chia to continue having a meaningful and reasonably active life even into their 90s.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: By the way, my mother-in-law celebrates her 100th birthday next week.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: These kind of initiatives can become a part of the Healthier SG community partnership.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: It would be wonderful to see how these can qualify or be recognised under the rewards of Healthier SG as well.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: With an ageing population, it may soon become an imperative for everyone to be equipped with care skills.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Perhaps that will come a time for everyone to be trained in basic nursing and care skills and be providing the services in their own families or communities or to be involved in some form of national community services.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: This could apply to young men as part of their National Service and for young ladies as part of their pre-IHL community service training.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: This can also apply to retirees as well.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: It could be a voluntary basis or perhaps even considered as some form of paid gig work of sorts.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: My third point: shortage of nurses and allied healthcare workers.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: When there are insufficient nurses and allied healthcare workers, the in-service staff including junior doctors all have to take up the slack, resulting in everyone overworking, experiencing burnout and mental wellness issues.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: In having to manage the COVID-19 response since 2020, our healthcare workers must likely added several years to their age.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Some ideas include: (a) broadening training and responsibilities for existing nurses, allied health professionals and pharmacists so that they can take on crucial roles alongside doctors.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: This can help make these pertinent roles more attractive to Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: A lot, I know, is already being done by MOH in this aspect but more still yet to be done.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: My point is that we have to align to pay for skills.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: When it comes to compensation, more is always welcome.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: That said, from the conversations I have had, what carries more weight when choosing nursing and allied health as careers is not exactly money.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: If they want to make lots of money, they will go and become investment bankers and so on.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: But what is important is being on a role that is respected and appreciated, having more flexibility so that work life balance can be better achieved and having the opportunity for career progression and personal growth, perhaps being able to say that living a life with a purpose.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: (c) the community can help by changing our mindset when it comes to perceiving and treating "service" staff.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Our nurses and allied healthcare professionals should be treated with every dignity, respect and gratitude.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: (d) designing human resource (HR) policies that offer opportunities for them to choose pathways to progress in their career toward further certifications and even degree qualifications, granting study leave and examination leave for those doing their part-time degree or part-time specialised training, much like what we do for the doctors.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: These staff often struggle with roster and they feel bad for requesting shifts.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: If we are serious about lifelong learning, this is something that needs to be addressed.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: It need not necessarily be fully paid leave but just provide some flexibility in rostering.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: (e) technology can automate repetitive work and augment the skills of the nurses and healthcare staff.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Singapore is well recognised for our innovations on the world stage as amongst the top dozen or so healthcare systems that leverage technology well.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Whether it is Robotic Process Automation (RPA) or artificial intelligence (AI) or data analytics, they have been proven to support positive patient outcomes, in addition to efficiency and effectiveness in the organisation.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Mindset change and ease of adoption are key challenges that need to be done.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: One good example is the use of sensors to read vital signs, reducing the time nurses and doctors have to spend going from patient to patient to take their vitals physically.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: I have got plenty to give but, due to short of time, I will just go straight to the point.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Jobs that are well assisted and enhanced with technology are more attractive especially for the younger generation.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: I am sure it is already doable for robots to serve the medication based on the barcode of the patient's tag and the day will come when barcode can read our retina and serve out the correct medication.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: (f) design scheduling system that can accommodate flexible shifts/hours.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Such a system will be very attractive for staff who needs to juggle work with family and caregiving duties as well as studies as pointed out earlier.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Some of these nurses have had years of experience prior to their break and would like to rejoin the service but perhaps, are experiencing difficulty getting back their registration.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: With appropriate retraining, this would be a good pool of candidates to bring back into the workforce, at an appropriate level and not make them start with the junior nurses all over again.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: There is also a Nursing Career Conversion programme and this programme, I hear, has been pretty successful in terms of enrolment.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: It will be interesting to get the statistics on the number of jobs which get filled by the graduates of such programmes and schemes.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: (g) for foreign nurses and allied health staff, not being able to bring their family with them seems to be the biggest bugbear especially as other countries dangle that benefit.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: We know it is a challenge for Singapore but perhaps, MOH, Ministry of Manpower (MOM) and Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) can share the strategy for attracting and retaining foreign nurses and allied health professionals?

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Well, I hope that all parents can do our part to encourage our children who went overseas to attain their healthcare degrees and qualifications, to come home.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: I would recommend for MOH to do for nursing and allied health professionals, the same or similar as what is being done to attract overseas medical school graduates who are Singaporeans and Permanent Residents (PRs) to return and work here.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: I hear that our marketing campaign makes the graduates feel very much needed.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: (i) one last point on this issue of manpower shortage.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: We might want to incentivise qualified professionals who are Singaporeans and PRs schooled and qualified overseas to return to Singapore and take up the open positions and get themselves registered.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: I have heard anecdotal stories that Singaporean physiotherapists who are qualified to practise in Australia, cannot get registered in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Apparently, they are expected to have undergone the same breadth of training as Singapore-trained physiotherapists.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: In this way, we bring home another Singaporean son or daughter, who becomes a plus to our workforce.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Four, how can private sector play a part.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: There will always be senior doctors who, after their training, opt out of the public system, quit and go private.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: That is a perennial challenge for the public sector in the management of specialists.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: To have a Healthier SG, we need all hands-on deck.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: One suggestion is for private sector specialists to regularly attend to subsidised patients on a pro bono basis or subsidised rate or they could run free clinics for those assessed to be unable to pay.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Execution may not be easy but as during COVID-19, we see how the private sector healthcare was roped in and played an important role in complementing public healthcare resources.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: In this regard, we can learn from the legal community.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: With the Healthier SG, general practitioner (GP) doctors and family medicine clinics are going to be the key nodes of care, in the community.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: I am sure that MOH is constantly reviewing the split between various specialisation.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: It is quite clear that we should be encouraging more junior doctors to specialise in family medicine and pursue the path of becoming GPs or family doctors.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: From my understanding, family medicine is already a speciality.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: What will it take to attract more medical officers to choose the family medicine route?

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: How many training positions are there each year if we are successful in convincing medical officers that it is as good as any other specialisation?

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Private sector GPs and clinics must step up to offer specialisation traineeships for our junior doctors.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: And we probably need to look into pay gaps amongst these specialities.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: What will it take to motivate the GPs to engage and be part of the primary care network so that together, we can work toward a common goal of preventive health?

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Prevention and going upstream has been proven to be the best way to improve clinical outcome.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: For example, at Intermountain, they incentivise the primary care network to keep people out of hospitals as much as possible.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: In Singapore, we should perhaps look to modelling something similar.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: One of the issues that I hear often is that GPs are not set up to handle and cope with the increased administration and IT workload.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: It might be worth considering for MOH to set up a standardised platform or for an agency or a private sector to provide the administrative services required to be done at scale.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: It is important that the GPs step forward and engage themselves in the redesign of work processes and incentives that will help make Healthier SG implementation efficient, effective and most importantly, deliver on its intended purpose.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: The GPs need to lean in, to help themselves and to help reinvent primary care for our Singapore healthcare ecosystem, help technology to help our medical teams.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Ms Ang, you are at 19 minutes 40 seconds.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang
text: Who will be responsible for recruiting, training and managing all of them?

speaker: Ms Janet Ang
text: As I conclude, I cannot help but worry about our collective ability to transform at this pace.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang
text: To rush too much, risks the effort being channelled to the superficial, resulting in us getting the form and losing the substance.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang
text: We are blessed to have a healthcare system that is amongst the best in the world.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang
text: To all of you in and around healthcare, to quote Pope Francis, "Compassion is the heart of what you do.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang
text: You know that it is not just about good organisation but a heart of all that is listening, accompanying and supporting the people under your care." It is not an easy job but for most of you, it is a vocation.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang
text: So, a big thank you for your tireless efforts and contributions to keeping Singapore and Singaporeans health aware, ready, inclusive, resilient and dignified through every stage of our lives.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: The work group presented its findings and recommendations in March this year.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Their findings on the extent of abuse is troubling.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Healthcare workers are in a particularly vulnerable position.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Their job inherently involves interaction with people who are in need of some form of assistance or attention, or whom may even be in distress.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Many healthcare workers therefore internalise that some abuse is to be expected as they carry out their jobs and this often leads to under-reporting.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: In other words, many of these forms of abuse and harassment arise out of an expectation that the patient and/or the caregiver should be treated in a certain way, that they may have some entitlements that they are not getting or that they should have some level of service or timeliness.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: This prevalence of abuse against frontline service workers has also been found in other sectors.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: The critical question, therefore, is why do these abusers have these expectations and why do they think they think they can resort to shouting, making demeaning remarks or threatening to make complaints?

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: I wonder whether it is precisely because of the fact that our healthcare system is reputed to be one of the best in the world and whether it has something to do with the quintessential Singaporean aspiration towards efficiency and accountability.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Has this now become so ingrained in our people that it has become a basic expectation of all services and workers in Singapore?

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Then, when this expectation is not met, Singaporeans become frustrated as they feel that the system has failed them.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: In this regard, our success at being efficient and productive may have turned out to be a double-edged sword, because even falling slightly short can lead to backlash.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: One thing that stood out for me in the report was that one of the more prevalent types of abuse was threatening to file complaints or to take legal action against the worker.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Again, this appears to be an aberrant, twisted application of the whistle-blowing process, the desire to improve through feedback as well as the rule of law.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Are we becoming more litigious as a society and is it happening because we believe that any perceived slight or inconvenience can be remedied by litigation by complaining or through the courts?

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: All these affect the morale of the healthcare workforce and their ability to carry out their jobs.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: This included the threat from an abusive individual who threatened to look for her outside her workplace.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: He said – he said it in Mandarin, which I shall not try to say verbatim, but the translation of it is, "Singapore is so small.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Even mouse also can find." This is what I was told the translation is.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: When it comes down to our workers on the ground, what they are focused on is getting their job done.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Technology and processes have made us faster and better but there are also sometimes administrative processes that workers have to follow.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: For example, the Personal Data Protection Act now imposes certain requirements on data collection and processing that are necessary to protect personally identifying information.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Another example is that as our population ages, there will be an increasing need to appoint deputies.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: There are certain statutory procedures that must be complied with that caregivers may not fully understand.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: This could lead to frustration with hospital administrators and tempers could flare.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: As such, a key plank of the effort to prevent abuse and protect our healthcare workers should be to instill in patients, caregivers and members of the public that regardless of their frustration with administrative processes or perceived systematic inefficiencies, it is not acceptable to take out these frustrations on the workers who are merely working within the system that they find themselves.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: This goes beyond having mere statutory protections and penalties under the law.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: It requires that we adopt a societal mindset of civility and kindness instead of imperious expectation and entitlement.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: In fact, this is what the hon Member Dr Wan Rizal said earlier – that we need to have an all-of-society effort.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Japan, for example, has a culture of omotenashi, or selfless hospitality, which is seen as a microcosm of the Japanese mindset to be centred on care rather than expectation.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Omotenashi provides that good manners and a polite bearing are not just expected in interactions between individuals in social contexts but that they are also indications of respectability and good standing.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Principles include humility, patience, a quickness to apologise and an even tone in conversation.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: To emphasise omotenashi and ensure that this core Japanese characteristic is not lost amidst a modernising society, the Tokyo municipal government launched the Tokyo Good Manners Project in 2016, which is ongoing.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: MOH Holdings had already announced that it would be launching a national public education campaign to promote positive relationships of trust and respect between healthcare workers, patients and their caregivers.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: I truly hope that this campaign will be successful in reducing incidents of abuse, giving societal support to our healthcare workers and building our very own omotenashi.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Abuse of healthcare workers comes generally from two categories of individuals – patients and caregivers or family members of patients.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: As regards patients, healthcare professionals may find themselves in a conundrum.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Patients who are elderly, have mental health issues or who are in pain may sometimes turn abusive, including physically abusive.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Further to this, healthcare workers may also disengage from abusive patients by refusing unreasonable requests.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: I imagine that it will be challenging drafting the guidelines for this as it would have to balance the need to provide medical care to patients while, at the same time, protecting healthcare workers from physical, mental and emotional abuse.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Likewise, for caregivers and family members who may be distraught due to a medical emergency or condition of their loved one, there may also be instances where they turn abusive.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: My view is that while we can be sympathetic to family members in such situations, there should be zero tolerance if they turn verbally or physically abusive or harass healthcare workers.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
