text: While it is a part of the healthcare worker's role to provide support to these people, there is no overriding obligation of providing medical care to them.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: As such, the procedures to deal with abusive non-patients should be far stricter than those for abusive patients and should be actively enforced.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Supervisors and hospital management must stand by their workers.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: I was also heartened that Minister Ong has said that even the Minister will have their back and that healthcare workers should know this.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: I would also like to take this opportunity to support our healthcare workers and to thank them for all of the sacrifices that they have made and continue to make every day.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Our nurses, doctors, therapists, ah mahs, counsellors, pharmacists and administrators are in vocations that protect what is central to humankind – life and well-being.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Theirs are not merely noble professions but the noblest of all professions.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Let us therefore ensure that we do our very best to take care of them – that we take care of those who take care of us.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: To provide protection to its citizens against such contingent events, one might think that we could rely solely on private insurance companies.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: The argument is that risk-averse individuals would find it in their self-interest to purchase insurance policies that are offered at actuarially fair prices.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: However, because of asymmetric information, one side of the market has private information not readily available to the other side, leading to adverse selection.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: In a market that is characterised by adverse selection, more-costly-to-serve customers know who they are but sellers do not.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: The insurance company knows that among the potential pool of customers, some individuals are better risks than others but it does not know who the better risks are.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: The fact that insured individuals know their own risk level better than the insurer might cause those who are more likely to have an adverse health outcome to purchase an insurance policy, thus leading the insurer to lose money if it offers insurance.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: This national health insurance scheme has three important features.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Absent such a mandate, more healthy residents would have an incentive to opt out of buying coverage at a premium that reflects the much higher healthcare costs of less healthy residents.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: MediShield Life is administered by the CPF Board, which is a defined contribution social security system.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: In contrast to a defined benefit social security system where payroll taxes are collected from the working young to finance the benefits received by the retired old, CPF contributions form part of an individual's savings.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: In order for our national health insurance scheme to be financially sustainable, it is vital that the economy continues to generate good jobs.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: This is because the main source of financing the premium payments comes from an individual's MediSave Account.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: The Motion's call for a whole-of-Government approach is therefore very appropriate.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: The recent recommendation by the Advisory Committee on Platform Workers for platform companies to work with the Government to develop a mechanism for platform workers to make regular contributions to MediSave is also timely as it contributes to a financially sustainable national health insurance scheme.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It is imperative that our healthcare system is equipped to handle the unique challenges that comes with a super aged society.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We have to be forward-looking and address the issues now or we risk seeing our infrastructure and facilities unable to cope with demands.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This will impose a significant fiscal burden on Singapore in the future.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The Healthier SG initiative is undoubtedly a step in the right direction.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Social prescription is a key component in this.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We need to encourage our seniors to engage in activities that promote their overall health.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: There are plenty of free exercise and wellness programmes to do.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This is made available by Sport Singapore, PA and various social service agencies (SSAs), but we must rally the ground-up support and get active participation.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: What is being done in this respect to link up the two sides?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Otherwise, it is just another startup project – good for sound bites but may be ineffective in helping our residents.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Social prescription and healthcare must go hand in hand.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: There needs to be greater integration between health and social care.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Do healthcare professionals, including general practitioners (GPs) and their clinic assistants, know what kinds or types of exercise programmes exist or are provided by various organisations in the neighbourhood?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: If so, are they knowledgeable enough to recommend them to their patients?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Similarly, do our social service professionals know how to identify health-related issues in seniors and refer them to the appropriate healthcare professionals?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: A concept may look promising on paper, but the devil is always in implementation.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How do we help prepare healthcare staff outside of MOH who are to be part of this project?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We need to move away from the fear of over-medicalising healthcare and encourage greater collaboration between health and social care.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: A dedicated ministry can spearhead integrated policies relating to ageing, ensure that the needs of our seniors are met and make Singapore a great place to age in.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Second, Mr Deputy Speaker, Sir, we need better enablers to support care integration.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It is essential that we have an integrated system that allows for seamless collaboration between health and social care.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I mentioned about this in my previous Parliamentary speeches and during the Committee of Supply debate.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: For example, some clusters use Health Buddy where others use HealthHub.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: There are also a myriad of different computer systems across community, primary and tertiary healthcare providers, ranging from CCMS, Epic to Citrix.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Can we merge these IT systems to ensure that healthcare professionals have access to a unified platform to manage their patients' healthcare needs?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The same applies to merging GovTech systems and Integrated Health Information Systems (IHiS), ensuring that we have better data sharing between health and social sectors.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We must also explore ways to better enable data sharing between Government and SSAs on information regarding the wellness of seniors, both from the health and social sectors.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We should strive for a holistic view of the senior, encompassing both health and social aspects.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: What are the plans to scale up current pilots?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How can we ensure that telehealth is utilised effectively to provide comprehensive care for our seniors?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Third, as we seek to improve care integration for seniors.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We must also focus on further empowerment for care integration.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: One critical question that we must ask is this: can we better empower our seniors to better take care of themselves?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: To answer this question, we need to explore key messages and initiatives that seniors should look out for as they age.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This is similar to the child health booklet provided to primary school students and their parents.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: While we acknowledge this may not be feasible for those who are illiterate or have visual disabilities, it will still be a useful tool for many seniors and caregivers who need guidance.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: In fact, as our aged population becomes increasingly educated and literate in years to come, we expect much of this empowerment to require self-help and initiation on the part of our seniors.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Seniors would want to be empowered to make independent and informed decisions.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We need to nudge them in the right direction.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: A key move is to promote better transparency, push out more information on various health related topics, such as the cancer CDL list and insurance.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: In this regard, we should explore ways that the Silver Generation Office can help in this area.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: By providing seniors with the necessary information and resources, we can enable them to take better care of their health and well-being.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Ultimately, this will lead to better health outcomes and greater independence for our seniors.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: But what does a truly integrated system look like?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It would mean adopting a multidisciplinary and person-centric approach.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It entails doctors working closely with other health and social care professionals such as Allied Health Officers, social workers and even community befrienders to identify the common care needs for seniors and to offer integrated interventions.

text: I suspend the Sitting and will take the Chair at 3.40 pm.

text: Sitting accordingly suspended  at 3.22 pm until 3.40 pm.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Minister Ong Ye Kung and the MOH team would be glad to note that ChatGPT’s reply to me was, and I quote, “The Singapore healthcare system is often cited as one of the best healthcare systems in the world, known for its efficiency, high quality care and low healthcare costs.” That said, one cannot assume that this somewhat glowing review will remain status quo.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: If we are to reap the full harvest of meaningful and productive longevity, we must strive to close the glaring decade-long gap between health-span and lifespan.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: This is important, and I thought I ought to repeat this.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: If we want Singaporeans to not just live longer, but to live longer and better, we have a good 10-year health- and lifespan gap to close.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: And in the longer run, we must capitalise on the upsides of ageing.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: In 2017, Sport Singapore (SportSG) launched the Active Health national initiative to inspire Singaporeans to take ownership of their own health and well-being, and to foster greater community spirit through shared experiences.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: We wanted to nudge a mindset shift from one which is “deficit-focused”, that is, “I seek treatment only when I’m unwell”, to an “aspiration-focused” model of active, healthy living.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: In the latter model, everyone is empowered to live better, and to delay, or prevent the onset of chronic diseases.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Over the past decade, SportSG has been vigorously implementing the Vision 2030 recommendations.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: In an Active Health survey conducted in 2022, about 96% of the respondents gave a score of eight out of 10 when asked about the importance of health and wellness.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Yet, only 60% said they are confident of improving and/or maintaining their own health and wellness.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Many are unaware of their own health status and how they can easily take a small step towards an active, healthier lifestyle.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: I agree with Members that support is needed from all sectors of Singapore society to ensure that everyone can realise their health and wellness aspirations.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: One such concerted effort is the Queenstown Health District pilot.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Spearheaded by HDB, National University of Singapore (NUS) and the National University Health System (NUHS), the Health District seeks to increase healthy longevity and intergenerational bonding through the provision of health and wellness programmes for people of all ages.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: In Queenstown, facilitated by the Lion Befrienders, seniors participate in strength and balancing programmes, such as dance fitness, modified sports and virtual square-stepping exercise.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Seniors also take part in intergenerational sporting Friday activities, such as football, active-farming and dance fitness, designed for participants of all ages.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Students take part in an Active Health Classroom Champions programme that adopts a holistic approach to their health and promotes the participation of sport and physical activity beyond curriculum hours.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Under SportSG’s school sports partnership scheme, schools in Queenstown have introduced more multi-sport programmes to promote general health and well-being and social cohesion amongst students.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Families take part in workshops and programmes, such as Active Health Discovery Walk in the Park, which emphasises, for instance, the importance of resistance exercises in increasing muscle mass as they go for their regular walks.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: There are also programmes catered for the vulnerable and persons with disabilities.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: For instance, the SportCares FUN Starters multi-sport and Saturday Night Lights football programmes provide children and youth living in rental housing and other vulnerable communities, the opportunity to play and develop a lifelong habit in sports, improve fundamental movement skills and physical fitness as well as to instil a sense of belonging with the community.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Besides programming, SportSG collaborates with HDB to enhance infrastructure within the Queenstown Health District to enable residents to keep fit and to stay active.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: For example, an "Active Health Fitness Trail" with behavioural nudges designed by SportSG to develop strength, flexibility and balance as well as appropriate fitness equipment will be installed as part of the Neighbourhood Renewal Programme (NRP) to enhance the fitness and exercise spaces around the Mei Ling precinct in Queenstown.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Our objective is to enable people to understand their body composition, fitness and health status, and to learn tips from qualified Active Health Coaches on how to sustain an active and healthy lifestyle.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Residents come to our ActiveSG centres not just to do their workouts, but also to connect and to network.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Just last weekend, I joined hundreds of Queenstown residents as we bade a temporary farewell to our beloved Queenstown Sport Centre.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: The facility has served our residents very well for more than five decades, and has played host to decentralised National Day Parades, that was in the seventies, and was home to the Tanjong Pagar United Football Club and our National Water Polo team in the earlier days.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Indeed, sport and our sporting facilities also plays a critical role in place-making and the formation of a common identity.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: I would, therefore, like to call upon everyone to head down to our ActiveSG sport centres located island-wide, try out the various programs and activities, and to visit our Active Health Labs to kickstart your health and wellness journey today.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: To do this well, we need to work as a team.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Individual citizens can take the initiative to make a trip to the Active Health Labs, learn more about their own health and wellness, and consider working relevant fitness and dietary advice into their everyday lives.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Family members, too, can play a part by gently nudging loved ones to take the first step to taking charge of their own health and fitness by making the trip to the Active Health Labs.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Healthcare providers, on the other hand, can refer their clients to the Active Health Labs, to learn how to exercise safely with guidance from accredited training coaches.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: On the Government's end, SportSG will work with HPB and PA to ensure a steady pipeline of programmes, sport interest groups and social activities that healthcare providers can connect their clients to.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: (In Mandarin):   Singapore is one of the fastest ageing countries in the world.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Of course, we hope that Singaporeans can live long, but at the same time, we also hope that they can live healthily and meaningfully in their golden years.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: In order to achieve this, all stakeholders in our society will have to play a role.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Our aim is to enable people to understand their own body composition and health status, and to learn from qualified Active Health Coaches on how to sustain a healthy lifestyle.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: (In English): Sir, it is heartening to note that many recognise the importance of health and wellness.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Through Active Health, we hope to enable happier and healthier residents where they can live longer and flourish in "pro-social" spaces – where the young and old care for and nudge one another towards active living and healthy, purposeful longevity.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Before you do, I just like to point out that it is a last-minute request and to allow for better scheduling of Parliament Sittings, I would encourage all Members to continue to give us advance notice if they intend to participate in Parliamentary debates.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: This helps with the timetabling and the scheduling.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: I now call on you to give your speech, you may deliver it.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: I will speak about the steps we can take as a nation towards moving to a better balance in our expenditure on healthcare resources.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: I will share some details on why I think we can increase the carrying capacity of our healthcare system, perhaps, to some detriment in efficiency and some marginal pressure in costs that will pay off, I believe, in terms of greater long-term resilience.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: As others in this House have shared, and is well understood by this Government, our impending public expenditures on medical care would be substantially greater than what we have currently allocated for spending today.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: This is due predominantly to societal ageing and greater healthcare needs associated with the more elderly population.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: It is that, even at present, our healthcare system falls somewhat short of what we might reasonably expect for an economy at our stage of development.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: To be clear, I am not suggesting that our current system is fundamentally flawed, nor am I saying that it should be completely overhauled.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Indeed, I believe that we can justifiably be proud of the quality of care delivered by our existing system, which blends public as well as private components, and has proven to be remarkably cost-efficient in doing so, as Senior Parliamentary Secretary Eric Chua has just shared with this House.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: While I certainly prefer the balance to be tilted more toward a larger public share – a matter on which I had spoken about before, in the context of the debate on the amendments to the Healthcare Services Act in March this year – that is not the focus of my concerns today.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Rather, I wish to highlight what I believe is one glaring shortcoming that was raised by the COVID-19 episode: because we run our systems so lean, it has become fragile in the face of large, unanticipated, albeit, fully predictable shocks, such as the pandemic.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Here, a little philosophical discussion may, perhaps, be in order.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: The bread and butter function of economists is to maximise a given objective, subject to constraints.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: This, generally, means that we are constantly looking for optimal solutions and we are very happy when we find such solutions.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: My wife often makes fun of me, about how I gain enormous satisfaction by planning my visit to the grocery store along with all my other errands – pumping gas, drawing cash, "dabao" dinner – so that I can make one smooth, continuous trip.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: In this regard, economists are easily satisfied creatures.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: But there is another, equally tenable, worldview and that is one often held by engineers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Engineers do not look to wholly strip systems of inefficiencies.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: They recognise that redundancies are important, because while under normal conditions, such under-utilised elements may seem wasteful, they are mission-critical and can prevent the entire failure of the system during times of undue stress.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Accordingly, they build bridges that can bear far more weight than one might expect with normal traffic – and then add a little more.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: They design planes that can run with one engine, even when the other stops.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: They design power plants that can possess multiple fail-safes, so that they can keep the whole thing running while a compromised part is being repaired.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Of the four economies that have a lower coverage than we do, only one, Japan, has a significantly larger elderly share in its population.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: To be clear, this low bed count is not prima facie evidence that there is a problem with the present system.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: We need to look at the occupancy of said beds, and one could even make the argument that efficient recovery means that we are able to sustain a lower carrying capacity.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: In a response to a Parliamentary Question filed last year by my hon friend Mr Leon Perera, Senior Minister of State Janil Puthucheary shared that the target bed occupancy rate over the next five years was around 80%, which he added was generally recommended by academic communities as well as healthcare authorities.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: And in a statement to this House the year prior, he also explained that we have been able to ramp up ICU beds very quickly, as we did during the pandemic.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: But in that statement, he also acknowledged the need to ramp up ICU bed capacity, although he qualified this by pointing out that this process was non-trivial, being limited, principally, by the need to increase the medical personnel required to staff such beds.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: MOH has shared that it plans to roll out a new health campus in Woodlands, as well as another in Bedok, but the remaining projects are all expansions of current facilities.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Will the Minister be willing to share if these will be sufficient to cater, to not just anticipated increases in demand due to an aging population, but also relieve some of the existing capacity constraints faced?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Or will they be mainly focused on matching resources with new incoming demand, leaving current capacity largely unaltered?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: This brings us to what appears to be the key constraint: medical manpower.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: At present, we also have a comparatively low coverage of doctors and nurses.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Unsurprisingly, this has led to burn-out, stress and high turnover among our medical professionals, which others in this House have articulated.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: The solution appears straightforward and is uncontentious: we need to increase our supply of medical personnel.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Given this context, increasing supply calls for us to attract as well as retain global talent in the short term while looking for ways to expand domestically trained workers in the longer term.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: The practical manifestation of our limited beds and doctors is that wait times for admission to a ward has remained elevated at many facilities.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: This has been most chronic at Khoo Teck Puat Hospital, although we have seen spikes at Ng Teng Fong General Hospital as well as Sengkang General Hospital, which is located in the constituency that I represent.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: The question we should ask ourselves is this: are we willing to accept the status quo where our patients may occasionally need to wait for more than a day to be admitted to a hospital?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Perhaps, we think that this is a reasonable trade-off to keep overall medical costs down or we may use this fact as symptomatic of a need to increase the carrying capacity of the present system.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: For experienced doctors who have a long track record of working in other jurisdictions, we can simplify the application and accreditation process, perhaps, with designated processes based at MOH that would seek out such doctors and encourage them to apply.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: As we compete for global nursing talent with other advanced economies, many of whom are facing their own nursing shortages, it also makes sense to train more of our homegrown workforce to take this on.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: We could offer more generous terms for trainees.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: We could fully waive course fees, for instance, which, to be fair, is already relatively modest, on the condition that these trainees also work as nurses in Singapore for a certain duration after graduation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: This could also apply to those who would consider a mid-career switch.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: We can ensure that SkillsFuture funds not only fully cover conversion courses but also perhaps provide more credit for prior training.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: For example, early childhood educators and teachers surely would satisfy general courses in communications, critical thinking, data analysis and behavioural science, all of which are part of the nursing curriculum today.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Easing the supply pressure will require that we go beyond policies on the quantity dimension.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: At the simplest, this means that salaries in the field should rise.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: One existing limitation to more sustained increases in wages is that costs are already high.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: This, in turn, seems to be led by commercial rental rates for private hospitals, which can spill over into public pricing.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: The high rent is a function of – well, you guessed it – elevated land pricing.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: But it is not simply about higher wages – if these are simultaneously accompanied by longer hours.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: If anything, it would be better to increase the total number of doctors and nurses while keeping hours sane.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: The total wage bill will remain the same but the quality of care is likely to improve.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: We could also increase the number of tiers within nursing – the number is as many as five or six in other countries – from our present three of enrolled, registered and advanced practice nurses.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: This offers additional upward mobility pathways, making the profession more attractive for those contemplating entry.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: It is wise to adjust and adapt to impending needs at a time of relative calm rather than feel the need to "kelam-kabut" to make up for these during a future pandemic scenario.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Our own health account is like a bank account.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: The more we put in it, the more we can get out of it.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Investing in your health now will pay dividends for the rest of your life.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Most of us would agree that our children need to start healthy living habits from young and consistently practise healthy living in order to have the best chance of staying healthy and living life to the fullest.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Throughout their educational journey, students acquire knowledge, skills and attitudes to cultivate an active and healthy lifestyle and maintain it beyond their schooling years.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: At the preschool stage, MOE's Nurturing Early Learners (NEL) Framework emphasises holistic development by encouraging healthy habits and a positive attitude towards participating in physical activities.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: In schools, students learn about good health practices, such as regular exercise, sufficient sleep and healthy eating.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: During Physical Education (PE) lessons, they learn to play a variety of sports and games that equip them to participate in physical activities well into adulthood.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Our polytechnics have various health and wellness modules for our students while ITE has weekly PE curriculum.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: MOE schools and our Institutes of Higher Learning (IHLs) also provide opportunities for students to be physically active outside formal curriculum hours.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Students can take part in Co-Curricular Activities (CCAs) and join interest groups or sports clubs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: They can make use of sports facilities and equipment in schools and on campus to remain physically active.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: HPB works with schools and IHLs that wish to adopt programmes, such as the Active Youth Programme, to increase physical activity participation through regular contemporary workout sessions.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Nutrition is another critical aspect of physical health.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: All schools and IHLs actively promote healthy eating.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: In Food and Consumer Education lessons, lower secondary school students learn to plan and prepare healthier meals to suit their diets.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: The autonomous universities (AUs) also support healthy eating on campus by working with F&B vendors to provide healthier meals to the students.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Dr Wan Rizal spoke about the importance of mental health literacy for our students.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: For example, students learn about common mental health issues and the importance of help-seeking within the Character and Citizenship Education (CCE) curriculum.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: As the digital world has an impact on mental health, our students are taught ways to manage their social media use and develop healthy online peer support culture.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Families and the wider community play an important role in providing an enabling environment to support the adoption of healthy habits.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: At home, parents can help to reinforce and role model healthy habits.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: MOE shares practical and actionable tips with parents on building a positive family environment to develop strong physical, social, mental and emotional well-being for their children.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: These tips are shared with parents via MOE platforms, such as the Parent Kit, MOE Parenting IG and Parents Gateway.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: We have heard of positive stories from parents who play an active role to build a healthy lifestyle together with their children and, in doing so, have strengthened parent-child relationship.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: One father shared with us how he had started a routine to exercise with his child regularly, who had taught him the various types of sports and games that he learnt from PE lessons in school.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: With parents reinforcing and role modelling what their children are learning in school, I am confident that more children will develop healthy habits for life.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: We are heartened to see stakeholders, such as the Parent Support Groups (PSGs), COMPASS which stands for COMmunity and PArents in Support of Schools council, HPB and various social service agencies working in partnership to support parents on ways to strengthen children's health and well-being.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: We thank parents and our community partners for working with us to promote the well-being of our students.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: We look forward to continued and strengthened partnerships with more so that our children can build up their health accounts from young and live their lives to the fullest.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: As individuals, we need to take active steps to live healthier lives and minimise the risk of falling ill even as the Government builds a supportive environment to help us do this.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: I will speak about mental health, oral health and the healthcare IT infrastructure and digital tools to support individuals on healthy living.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: It lies along a spectrum and is multifaceted.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Mental health issues can arise from a range of factors, including physical health and social determinants.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Addressing these issues will require a collaborative and integrated approach that involves multiple stakeholders from the health, social, education, workplace and community sectors.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: These teams provide mental health education to residents and bring care, such as mental health screening, assessment and therapy, closer to home, where there is less stigma and individuals feel safe to seek help.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Prof Koh Lian Pin spoke about mental health in academic settings.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: HPB has worked with Institutes of Higher Learning (IHLs) to establish peer support structures.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Training is provided in empathetic listening and basic mental health first aid skills to support one's peers who show signs of emotional distress.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: In addition, those who wish to learn about mental health and self-care tips can access MindSG, a portal for mental health and well-being resources that are curated by mental health experts.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: It is important to address mental health issues that affect us at the workplace, whether that workplace is an academic setting or otherwise.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Dr Tan Yia Swam shared her experience as a junior doctor where there were occasions when she worked for more than 24 hours a day when she was on call.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: The public healthcare clusters have been piloting shorter call hours for junior doctors in selected departments as well as using electronic logging and surveys to monitor junior doctors' working hours.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: This is a complex subject which requires a fundamental relook at manpower deployment and the sharing of responsibilities between senior and junior doctors.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: This will take some time to study and work out and we are engaged on this matter.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Dr Tan Yia Swam and Prof Koh Lian Pin shared about the importance of mental health education and de-stigmatisation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: HPB launched the "It's OKAY to Reach Out" campaign in October 2021 to normalise the topic of mental health by building awareness and encouraging conversations.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: The campaign in 2022 was focused on youths to help them overcome their hesitation to seek support and address their concerns about seeking help.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Activities such as teacher-guided class discussions were brought to mainstream schools and Institutes of Higher Learning (IHLs).

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Outreach efforts to promote mental health awareness and literacy among Singaporeans have continued through online efforts and in-person programmes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: In addition to all this, the National Council of Social Services (NCSS)' Beyond the Label (BTL) movement which was launched in 2018 by NCSS, continues.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: In the next phase, BTL 2.0 moves to inspire action.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: NCSS has brought together 26 partners across the people, public and private sectors to promote and enable help-seeking and help-giving behaviours in schools, workplaces and the community.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: There were over 950 responses, with feedback from groups such as youths, parents, persons with mental health conditions, service providers, employers and community agencies.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: The respondents were supportive of all the recommendations and the task force will be releasing a short report of the consultation's findings soon, even as we commence with the implementation plans for these recommendations.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: One of the recommendations is to implement a tiered care model for mental healthcare delivery.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: This is a framework that matches the level of care to the degree of mental health need, allowing for a more effective allocation of mental health services based on the severity and complexity of an individual's needs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: As part of the public consultation, we received very useful feedback on the implementation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: One example would be, for the tiered model to work well, service providers need to be sufficiently competent to fulfil their roles and responsibilities.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We completely agree, that for this tiered care model to be implemented effectively, an important aspect is to ensure adequate competencies and standards amongst all mental health practitioners.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: So, we have the National Mental Health Competency Training Framework Workgroup.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: The framework that they are developing will guide mental health practitioners on the knowledge, skills and competencies necessary to deliver quality and effective care.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: It will apply to all practitioners, from lay responders such as peer supporters, to mental health professionals, including nurses, social workers and counsellors, amongst others.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: In addition, there is already a system in place to safeguard professional practice today.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Mental health professionals are regulated through professional boards and councils and set practice standards through professional associations.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: For example, psychiatrists, nurses and occupational therapists are regulated by the Singapore Medical Council, the Singapore Nursing Board and the Allied Health Professions Council, respectively.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Professional associations such as a Singapore Association for Counselling and the Singapore Psychological Society provide guidance on the professional and ethical conduct for counsellors and psychologists respectively.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: There is also the need to help individuals with mental health needs access the appropriate services in a timely manner.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Some respondents from the consultation felt that there was value in having more than one way to deliver a service to take into account user preference.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We are developing a number of service modalities such as hotlines, text messaging, in-person services and digital resources to ensure that there are sufficient and different ways for people to access these first-stop touch points for mental health.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: The Government has introduced initiatives to ensure the access to affordable and quality health care for Singaporeans such as through the Community Health Assist Scheme (CHAS).

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Most oral health needs of these population groups can be met by general dentists at the polyclinics, CHAS clinics and private dental clinics.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Individuals with complex needs and those with medical conditions or multiple morbidities that require a higher level of care are cared for and can be cared for by specialists at our National Specialty Dental Centres and the hospital dental clinics.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: To facilitate access, MOH has worked with MSF to list the details of dentists and private dental clinics providing special care dentistry services so as to raise the awareness regarding the availability of services for persons with disabilities.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Additionally public-private partnerships in addition to the existing ones like Enabling Village, Agape Village, HealthServe and Saint Andrews Mission Hospital will be further explored to better serve the primary medical and dental care needs of underserved communities including migrant workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: For our migrant workers, the Ministry of Manpower (MOM) will also continue to explore working with key partners such as NGOs to facilitate accessible dental care for migrant workers and provide oral health education through Project MOCCA, the Management of Oral and Chronic Conditions and Ailments.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Project MOCCA was launched by MOM last year and is a preventive health framework to enhance the care of oral and chronic diseases among workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: And in this, MOM works closely with partners such as MigrantWell Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We recognise the efforts of independent volunteer initiatives that provide dental services within the community, intermediate and long-term care settings and in special needs organisations.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: To improve the coordination of these services, we will be encouraging larger volunteer associations to help provide a platform for communication, for sharing of resources and for coordination.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: As the practice of dentistry constantly evolves with changes in population demographics, advances in technology and shifts in care approaches, the local dental landscape will shift accordingly.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: To better support dental professionals and other healthcare and non-healthcare professionals providing care for older adults and persons with special needs, we will look into the development of clinical practice guidelines and appropriate care guides to help establish standards of care and promote better health outcomes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Additionally, we will continue to review our subsidy framework and award scholarships for residency training programmes in the various disciplines of dentistry so as to ensure our dental workforce can continue to meet the oral health needs across all ages and care settings.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Members of the House have raised this in past Parliamentary sessions such as the White Paper for Healthier SG and also at the Committee of Supply 2023 debate.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: One key system will be the National Electronic Health Record System (NEHR), which is a common platform that captures selected patient health information from various healthcare providers and allows providers to view these health records for patient care.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Mr Gerald Giam asked about the implementation of security enhancements for NEHR.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: The NEHR has been subjected to cybersecurity reviews, infrastructure vulnerability scans and application penetration tests.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: On the matter of IT support for GP clinics, that Mr Gerald Giam also raised.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We do want GPs to use a Clinic Management System (CMS) that supports their daily operations well and connects to key IT systems, to save them time on administration.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Ms Ng Ling Ling and Mr Yip Hon Weng also raised the need to empower Singaporeans with more knowledge and support to manage their health better.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We will do this through tools such as the HealthHub and Healthy 365 applications.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We will explore how we can reflect more results in these platforms.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Residents and their authorised caregivers can also use HealthHub to book and manage their medical appointments across all public healthcare institutions, as well as to enrol in Healthier SG and view their Health Plan.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Residents can use Healthy 365 to see and sign up for nearby healthy lifestyle programmes, track their physical activity and collect health points from clocking steps and making healthier food choices.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We will continue to enhance such digital tools to help residents sustain good health and well-being.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I want to thank Dr Tan Yia Swam, Dr Shahira and Mr Abdul Samad for tabling this Motion, and pointing out passionately that health is everyone's concern, and it is only with everyone’s action that we can improve the health of individuals and our nation.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I would also like to thank all the Members of Parliament and representatives of Ministries who have, through your speeches, supported the various health-related policies and also given suggestions for improvements.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This includes Healthier SG, our preventive care strategy; championing the well-being of our healthcare workers; developing more centralised IT systems; group buying of drugs with private doctors; ensuring that healthcare remains affordable for everyone and so on.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Members have also raised a range of challenges and frustrations of the healthcare system.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Indeed, healthcare is probably one of, if not the most, complex public service systems in our whole public service.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It will be unrealistic of me if I were to say we have a solution to every problem that you have raised.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Even if we have, theoretically, it is not practical to implement them all.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We will need to work within the budget and time resources we have, our management bandwidth to plan and effect change, our people's appetite to accept changes.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Together, they represent a major transformation of our healthcare system in the medium-term.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But before I talk about these priorities, let me first address three specific issues on healthcare that were raised by Members: manpower, financing and as Prof Jamus Lim just raised, healthcare capacity.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It is last minute, but I will respond to you.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: At the heart of any healthcare system are the workers.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Several Members of Parliament such as Dr Tan Yia Swam, Ms Janet Ang, Dr Wan Rizal, Mr Gerald Giam, Mr Abdul Samad and Mr Raj Joshua Thomas have spoken about the issues confronting them.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We have to support healthcare workers as much as we can.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The NTUC and Healthcare Services Employees' Union (HSEU) have been fervent supporters for the welfare of healthcare workers.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Ms Thanaletchimi, President of HSEU, used to be a Nominated Member of Parliament in this House and spoken about it many times.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The partnership between the People's Action Party (PAP) Government and the Labour Movement is a strong institutionalised arrangement, and MOH looks forward to our continued partnership in advancing the welfare of our healthcare workers.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We will internally benchmark not just the pay but also taxes – because it varies across countries – and also the living conditions and rental.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But I suggest we do this internally, because competition is now so tough, you do not want to benchmark and then show everybody.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But we certainly want to benchmark and make sure we are competitive.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Right now, in fact, rental becomes a problem for foreign nurses to come to Singapore and out of pocket expenses are high.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: These are some things we need to address to make sure we are competitive.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: For local healthcare workers, we are looking forward to the inflow of the latest batch of polytechnic graduates who, I think, just graduated and they will be joining the workforce and our hospitals soon.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Mr Abdul Samad had feedback about interns not getting paid for their internships.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: All Institute of Technical Education (ITE) and polytechnic nursing students are given allowances for their internship attachments.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: However, for certain healthcare-related courses, such as Biomedical Science, allowances are an arrangement left between employers and the school to set, and practices can differ across health clusters.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But given the Member's feedback, let us look into the specific instances where our public health institutions do not offer internship allowances.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: As for foreign healthcare workers, it takes time to conduct selection and examinations overseas and for the shortlisted candidates to move here.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: A few Members of Parliament (MPs) have suggested granting PR status to their dependents as well.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: For everyone in our healthcare workforce, we will need to ensure their well-being.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I am glad many MPs spoke up against abuse and harassment of healthcare workers.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This is one of the top issues in the minds of our healthcare workers.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I think, in general, I would say, to be fair, the regard and appreciation for healthcare workers has generally gone up amongst our society post COVID-19.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And for the majority of the public, they are appreciative and respectful towards our healthcare workers.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Those who physically assault, threaten or hurl vulgar and condescending remarks against healthcare workers, I think is really a small minority.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But because the acts are so egregious, it feels like a big thing.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This is unfair to healthcare workers and unfair to the great majority of the public who respect our healthcare workers.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I will not elaborate what it entails as I have spoken about this before.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But since the announcement of the policy, I have noticed some reactions.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: First and the best is that most members of the public support the policy.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Second, a few raised concerns that there were occasions where healthcare workers did not behave appropriately.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: There are always a minority of black sheep.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But there are appropriate channels to report such matters and the hospital management will look into them seriously.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Some have said that one of the root causes of abuse is the heavy workload at the hospitals and long waiting times, and therefore, we should address that first.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We are doing what we can to alleviate the situation at the hospitals post COVID-19.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But heavy workload cannot be an excuse for anyone to physically or verbally abuse our healthcare workers.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Mr Raj Thomas mentioned that another reason is expectations are high and when it is not met, people get upset.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It is totally all right to have expectations and to demand good service.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: By all means, do that, but there is no need to abuse healthcare workers should service delivery fall short.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I should say that notwithstanding the heavy workload and the occasional abuse and harassment, most healthcare workers I have met – and I hope it is not just because I am Minister – remain positive, professional and passionate about their jobs.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Ms Koh Fang Qi, for example, was a senior staff nurse in Khoo Teck Puat Hospital since 2015.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Over the years, she dealt with many abusive patients and next-of-kin, but she continued to calmly handle each one with empathy and became an expert in this field.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Once, she witnessed a junior nurse being abused physically and verbally by the next-of-kin of a patient.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, she bravely stood up, managed the situation and escalated the incident to the authorities for follow-up and remained calm throughout the incident.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And despite all these challenges, you can tell she loves her job.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: She continues to treat patients and their loved ones with care and kindness.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: She constantly shares her knowledge and experience dealing with abuse cases with her colleagues.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The test of zero-tolerance policy is in the second half of this year when we have guidelines and supervisors to disengage abusive patients or most likely, their next-of-kin.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I do expect some to write to the Ministry to complain to me why do our supervisors and nurses act this way.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We will make sure that we will effect the consequences only for the most genuine cases and care will always be prioritised.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Should I get a complaint, I will back our ground supervisors; and healthcare workers.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Should it comes to this Chamber, because I think some of the residents will complain to their MPs: "why MOH act like that, can they appeal against this, they disengaged with me and I was just demanding good service." When the time comes and test comes, I hope to have the support of this House.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We will be careful and we will do it judiciously if we ever have to disengage an abusive patient or next-of-kin, so, I seek the support of the whole House.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Mr Leong Mun Wai made a few points yesterday.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I am glad he agreed with our policy to use MediFund to support low-income families.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: However, Mr Leong also delivered a political statement yesterday.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: He declared the Progress Singapore Party (PSP)'s position that Government ought to spend more in healthcare like other OECD countries.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: First, it is widely known that spending more on healthcare does not mean better health outcomes.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Since Mr Leong is benchmarking ourselves against OECD countries, let us just cite two examples, US and UK.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: They are spending about 17% and 10% of their GDPs on healthcare, compared to us, 4%.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Yet, US and UK continue to face high incidence of chronic illnesses, high obesity rates and their expected lifespans are lower than Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I was inspired by Mr Eric Chua and also checked out ChatGPT: "what do you think of the US system, what do you think of the UK system".

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In the US, healthcare is very expensive, despite spending 17% of their GDP.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In the UK, the National Health Service (NHS) is crushed down by the workload.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The waiting times are far longer than in Singapore, despite spending 10% of their GDP on healthcare.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We have delivered good health outcomes given what we are spending.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The second point, for whatever we are spending, we are able to make healthcare affordable for middle to lower-income groups.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Today, about seven in 10 of Singaporeans in subsidised wards do not have to pay any out-of-pocket expenses.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Eight in 10 pay less than $100 cash out-of-pocket; nine in 10 pay less than $500 in cash out-of-pocket.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, when Mr Leong asked the Government to spend more to lower out-of-pocket expenses further, he really meant to channel resources to unsubsidised patients, that is, those staying in A class wards or private hospitals.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This is where the big bucks and the big expenditure are, and it will push our healthcare expenditure and spending to the levels of the OECD countries.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Third, while Mr Leong asked Government to spend on healthcare, he failed to mention that Government expenditure ultimately has to be raised from the people through taxes.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Mr Leong had not made any mention of where PSP will get the funding from.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Fourth, the fact is that we are already spending more and more on healthcare.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This is driven by an ageing population, who is also getting sicker.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: MOH already has the second largest Ministry budget, after Ministry of Defence (MINDEF).

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In the coming years, our challenge is not to spend more, but to ensure we do not go the way of many OCED countries, with the healthcare fiscal burden spiralling and escalating out of control.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This is the S+3Ms approach, which has worked quite well.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We now combine this with a very important strategy in Healthier SG and our effort to enable ageing in communities, so that we can avoid sickness and reduce our disease burden even as our population ages.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Mr Leong also talked about the seemingly large balances in the Pioneer Generation (PG) and Merdeka Generation (MG) Funds, and concluded that more subsidies can therefore be given to PG and MG members.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Both Funds were sized based on the projected lifetime cost of the benefits, and accounting for inflation and interest accrued.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: To illustrate, the oldest and youngest MG member is about 73 and 64 years old.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: PG members will be at least 10 years older, with the youngest at 74 years old now.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: They still have quite a bit of runway ahead of them and we do expect many of them to live until 90 or 100 years old.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, their lifetime benefits need to be funded from the MG and PG Funds.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But the Government will continue to regularly review the adequacies of these two Funds.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Third issue is healthcare capacity that Assoc Prof Jamus Lim just raised.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We agree that 80%, 85% occupancy rate is probably ideal.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And you do not need an engineer to conclude that you must have redundancy in your system.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It is something that I think we all agree to.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Of course, there will be crunch during COVID-19.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It was an emergency, it was a crisis of a generation.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I do not think any country or any system can plan for that kind of capacity to cater to a crisis.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But post-crisis, we do have a crunch today.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I think in time, researchers and clinicians will study why.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: One is that there is some kind of immunity debt – more old folks are getting infected with viruses, bacteria post-COVID-19.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And when they do, they fall quite sick and they actually stay in hospitals for quite long.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And that pushes up average length of stay.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Another reason, which is a possible one, is that during COVID-19, too many of our seniors decided to hide at home, afraid to come out.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: There were no more community activities, which actually is so crucial to keep them healthy.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And then, when they get infected, they stay in the hospital for very long.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The 15% increase in utilisation alone explains why we have a crunch now.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And it is happening not just in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Every country is facing a crunch in their beds.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: All of us agree we must have redundancy but all of us are facing a crunch, including and especially in OECD countries, despite their higher bed to population ratio.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Many of our projects have been delayed due to COVID-19.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We have to catch up but some things cannot be rushed.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, sometime this year, the Integrated Care Hub at Novena will open.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The Woodlands Integrated Health Campus, by end of the year, may have one ward open; hopefully, next year more wards will open.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And then we have the redevelopment of Alexandra Hospital and the eastern regional hospital Assoc Prof Jamus Lim talked about.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We have the redevelopment of SGH campus that is ongoing.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Although it is an existing campus, it is a significant redevelopment with many more beds added.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Two, is to build more Transitional Care Facilities (TCFs), which I have explained before.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Today, in our hospitals, there is still quite a number of seniors who are staying there not because of medical reason, but because of social reasons.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: TCFs have rehabilitative care and good medical facilities, and we can allow those who are stable to move to TCFs, thus freeing up acute beds.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, we are building that up quite actively.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
