text: A clinical practice guideline as well as care pathways are needed to help ensure quality and appropriate care is offered.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Complex cases with multiple health and behavioural problems can be seen in the hospital settings and milder cases can be referred to a network of dentists in GP clinics.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Complex cases can also be sent to GPs once they are stabilised.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Number three: the lack of access to dental care in elderly and special needs facilities.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Some of our communities and organisations serving vulnerable persons have taken the lead to develop their own dental capacities.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Even fewer homes have a fixed brick-and-mortar clinic run by a volunteer dentist when manpower is available.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: An example is the Hospice Care Association where a dental clinic was built in their newest day hospice Oasis@Outram.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: On the special needs front, Movement for the Intellectually Disabled of Singapore (MINDS) Developmental and Disabilities Medical Clinic was launched last year and is already working towards providing dental screening and referral services for patients.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: This has the potential to scale as MINDS open their cross-disciplinary Health Hubs.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: However, the lack of coordination between volunteer groups is also a major issue.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: This results in inefficient allocation of resources, such as manpower, and unmet needs in homes yet to be served.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: For someone with an autism spectrum disorder, going to an unfamiliar place for dental care can be a difficult experience.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Without onsite services, patients have to be ferried to primary care services, which may sometimes require costly private ambulances.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Treatment in clinics outside is limited by cross-institutional restrictions of data sharing, higher costs in specialised services and long waiting times to be treated, plus many more.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Therefore, it is beneficial that dental needs of the seniors and special needs persons to be managed "in place".

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Such clinics will also divert the efforts away from elective treatment such as dental aesthetics, and instead focus on primary needs – increasing their efficiency and cost-savings.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Funding is an important aspect of support as dental services have a high capital cost.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Other aspects of support could be flexibility in administration and licensing.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: However, until now it is still not approved here.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: We, however, still do have a shortage of dentists who volunteer and treat this population.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: To ingrain the spirit of volunteerism and service, we could have dental officers serve short postings while serving out their bond, to treat these elderly and special needs patients.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: This could also be extended to other vulnerable groups such as the migrant workers.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: This would hopefully encourage them to do the same when their bond has completed.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: The dental healthcare of vulnerable groups such as the migrant workers and the unique needs of the elderly and special needs populations should not be overlooked.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Nevertheless, I thank fellow NMP Dr Tan Yia Swam for allowing me to take part in the team rising this Motion.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: As I represent the voices of the working people, there are two main areas that my speech will focus on, namely, the welfare of healthcare workers and the challenges of enticing young Singaporeans to embark on a career in the healthcare sector – they are the future of our healthcare workforce.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: We call on those who are not members yet to quickly join the unions.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Unions will not just represent your voice at the workplace, but will also be your voice for a reason.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: While the healthcare industry is not within my purview, I have nonetheless reached out to the leaders of both HSEU and SMMWU to get their feedback on their members' concerns challenges and aspirations, both in the near- and the long-term future.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: With the recent pandemic, we realise how much our healthcare workers are doing for Singapore behind the scenes.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Indeed, the hours are long and from time to time, they are on the receiving end of abuse by families of the patients.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: The question is, why should it take a pandemic only for us to realise the importance of healthcare workers?

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Why do we need a pandemic to learn how to appreciate them?

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: It is only in periods of crises that we know the importance of these frontline workers.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Just like myself in the power industry, it is only when there are tariff hikes or power failures that we start to realise the importance of a stable and reliable power supply which we have taken for granted in our daily lives.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Do not be ashamed to deny this reality in this real world.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Many good suggestions and ideas were proposed by all in this Chamber for us to remind ourselves on leading a healthier lifestyle.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: While the focus was on developing healthy lifestyle, we should not forget the efforts of those who help us to develop healthier lifestyles, namely, our healthcare workers.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Let us be aware of the challenges faced by the healthcare workers, including those by our administrative and support staff, not just doctors and nurses who are facing patients directly.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Let us not forget the equally critical roles of those supporting at various other departments like radiology, pathology and more.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: This, then, brings me to focus on the welfare of healthcare workers now and preparing the future generation to serve in this industry.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Prior to this Sitting, I reached out to not just the two unions, but also current friends in my network, as well as fellow Singaporeans, who observed first-hand the hard work of our healthcare workers.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: We acknowledge that while the Ministry has done their part to better support this group of workers via the hospitals' management, there are still areas that can be further improved like shift work, wages and more.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Let us not wait until an unforeseen incident happens before we start to investigate.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: We need to ensure that shift rosters pay close attention to rest time in between, as we need physically alert workers at all times to attend to patients and support doctors.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: I feel strongly for this because my daughter is one of the thousands of healthcare workers.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: I have witnessed first-hand the long working hours that she has had to go through during her past 10 years at Sengkang Hospital.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Sometimes, I feel that it is not about the corporate shift policy, but the line managers who plan the rosters who may be biased toward their preferred choice of workers.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: She left recently and also shared with me that about half of her colleagues in the same team had also left much earlier.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: She is now embarking on the new journey at a new workplace.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: I did not raise this flag earlier as I was still doing my checks with my close friends within the sector.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: While doing my checks, I then recall this same issue was raised many years earlier at some dialogue sessions, and incidentally, my daughter also suffered the same fate.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Let us not paint internships like another day at school.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: It is not and will never be the same between academic and work experiences.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Let us not make our children, the workforce of the future, a source of free labour for today.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: This will mean healthcare workers may be able to relocate to their preferred hospitals near their homes, or get better pay, or even both.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Are we prepared for the pipeline of Singaporeans wanting to work in this healthcare sector, especially the young ones?

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: While we remain open to foreign healthcare workers to help supplement our resident workforce, what are the steps in place to ensure that there will be sufficient Singaporeans to be the core of our healthcare workers?

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: The above concern also represents a few of the many concerns that were shared with me by my fellow brothers and sisters in the unions.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: While much have been said for those at hospitals, let us not forget the healthcare workers at our neighbourhood polyclinics.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: The stress that they face at work is equivalent to those working in hospitals.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: This really stretches them and even the doctors there.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Separately, there are those that hope that polyclinic operations can soon be reduced to a five-day work week upon review of operating hours.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: On the lighter note, I do understand the ongoing tripartite efforts around the protection and prevention of abuse and harassment of our fellow healthcare workers.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: More severe action must be taken against any such abuse towards our healthcare workers, regardless of the magnitude.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: (In Malay):   In our journey towards preparing for an ageing population, we ramped up our healthcare plans inclusive of fellow healthcare workers.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Equipping the current ones with new knowledge and skillsets is vital in view of job demands and labour shortage.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: We need trained and caring healthcare workers to look out and take care of our ageing Singaporeans, both in hospitals and community homes.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: This job requires not just physical strength but also demands mental toughness when faced with difficult patients and challenging caregivers.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: As mentioned in my English speech earlier, there were, are and will be challenges for all of us.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Please note that there are two unions, HSEU and SMMWU, that are your voices to hear and speak for you about your workplace challenges.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Your unions are aware of your workplace challenges and will try their very best to advocate for your interest ranging from workplace matters to the provision of other welfare benefits.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Do not be shy to provide feedback because I know that my union brothers and sisters will always to be there for you.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: This call has been made repeatedly by Members of the House and I hope that it will not be taken lightly.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: If the above practice is not stopped, it could hinder young Singaporeans from joining this meaningful sector.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: We need more young Singaporeans to join this sector as we prepare for an ageing population.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: New hospitals are being built and they appreciate the efforts of my fellow union brothers and sisters from HSEU and SMMWU who are working with management partners to upskill their members and workers for the advanced mode of today's work and preparing for the future.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Please also ensure that our workers who have gone through such training will have better wages and better work prospects than before.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: (In English): Once again, I call on the relevant parties to remind ourselves about the importance of this group of healthcare workers and doctors, and never be shy to appreciate and say thank you to them whenever you visit hospitals, both restructured and private, polyclinics and even neighbour clinics.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: On behalf of all my fellow leaders from the Labour Movement, we would like to thank you for your efforts to look out for our families, friends and fellow Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Once again, do not forget to join the union because for the union – members first, workers always.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In fact, I have no doubts that the Government is committed to supporting healthcare beyond the COVID-19 pandemic.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Where I think the Government needs to continue to be vigilant is how this Budget is being spent and, more importantly, if it is translating to better health outcomes for our ageing population.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In addition, I cannot agree more with the NMPs that health for Singaporeans must be a whole-of-Government effort.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I will push further to say that it must be a whole-of-society effort.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I am a firm proponent of the Healthier SG initiative, having visited various parts of Netherlands, the United Kingdom and the United States a few years back on their healthcare systems to manage increasing chronic disease burdens in ageing populations of advanced countries like ours.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: GPs in Singapore, who are in the heart of the Healthier SG movement have, however, not been the centre of gravity in how our Government ensures delivery of good healthcare until recent years.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I cite an example of a very hardworking GP in my Jalan Kayu constituency.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: He has a GP clinic situated at the basement of a HDB block, a bomb shelter built by HDB and leased out to this clinic for many years.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: During the COVID-19 pandemic, as a Public Health Preparedness Clinic, he was given a temporary booth at the vacant void deck as his clinic stepped up to help in the administering of COVID-19 tests and vaccinations.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It was proven then that senior residents could access this clinic more readily with the void deck space, instead of the basement bomb shelter space which can only be accessed through a stairway.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The Singapore Civil Defence Force (SCDF) could not approve the clinic to install a wheelchair lifter down the flight of stairs.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Extending a lift to this basement clinic will need to wait for HDB's Lift Upgrading Programme, with no definite plan or timeline in sight.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: With the GP, I appealed to HDB to provide the vacant void deck space permanently to this GP Clinic.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Even if he manages to raise the amount, we were informed that the approval is further subject to agreement by the URA, Building and Construction Authority and SCDF.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Help doctors to help patients more and to do administration less.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This example I cited is just one of several that I have experienced while rallying GP clinics in my constituency to support Healthier SG, so that our residents can start their preventive health journey early with a trusted family doctor as exhorted by the Government.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: More handshakes across agencies under different Ministries for a less onerous and time-consuming workflow must be made with a whole-of-Government mindset if we want to see GPs embracing Healthier SG to help this multinational strategy succeed.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Last week, some of us were informed of a message that some community groups in a western part of Singapore have received from a good public hospital.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: ED doctors were operating as fast as they could with admission waiting time increasing and about 100 patients waiting for beds.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Their plea is for grassroots volunteers to help spread the message of not going to emergency wards unless necessary and to consult the GP clinics first if their conditions are stable.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Lastly, my point on not only the need for whole-of-Government commitment, but also whole-of-society actions for maintaining health in our ageing population.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Government funded clinical trials must speed up and extend to private GP space.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Chronic diseases are silent diseases, and complications in the form of heart attacks and strokes are too late for Singaporeans to know that their health is not in a good shape.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Many of the remote vital sign monitoring technology has been clinically proven to have better health outcomes for specific segments of chronic disease patients, but I see two constraints slowing its proliferation in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: One, operational trials to smoothen end-to-end data transmission between patients and primary healthcare teams, and care team workflows for responses to anomalies in the vital signs; and two, consent procedures for individuals to decide on the extent of releasing their personal vital signs data to their trusted doctors, public or private, and supporting teams, including community organisations like Active Ageing Centres.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Our rapidly ageing population is causing demand for health and social care to increase dramatically.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Yet, Singapore is facing a high attrition rate of nurses.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: One of the reasons why nurses in Singapore have reported to be resigning is because of their heavy workload and stress, which is caused, in large part, by the manpower shortage.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Urgent measures are needed to address this manpower shortage.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: We need to encourage more Singaporeans to choose health and social care as a career, so as to boost the pipeline of future professionals in this field.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I highlighted in my speech on Singapore's COVID-19 response in March that nurses in Singapore are often still seen as the assistants to doctors instead of being professionals in their own right.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: We need to boost the image of the profession and enhance societal esteem for nurses and allied healthcare workers.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Nurses should be granted more autonomy and entrusted with higher level responsibilities.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Schools should highlight careers in health and social care early to students.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Professional associations should come up with materials and videos highlighting the careers in this field and share them with schools to disseminate to their students.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I agree with Member Dr Tan Yia Swam's call just now for a repository of articles on navigating the healthcare system – and I hope she starts her blog again so that we can continue to tap on her knowledge.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This is so that students' interest in health and social care careers can be sparked early, and they can start working towards choosing suitable subjects as they move up to Secondary 3.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: As I mentioned in my speech on the education system in April, schools should move away from sorting students according to their grades and towards allowing students to take subject combinations based on their interests.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This is how we can continue to raise up a generation of future healthcare professionals who love what they do and are passionate about their work.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: IHLs could develop guidebooks to help local students prepare themselves for their eventual applications to these institutions.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: These guidebooks could include information on the subjects they need to take in school, the grades they need to obtain and the co-curricular and extracurricular activities they need to get involved in to best prepare themselves to get admitted to the institution and major of their choice.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: For example, this guide could recommend that students take certain subject combinations, join the science club, find opportunities to conduct scientific research, write and publish research papers, or work as an intern in a health or social care institution during their school holidays.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: It should provide guidance on how to search out these opportunities and work with professional health and social care associations to create these opportunities for students.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: These could all help our students focus early on pursuing their area of interest in health and social care and better prepare them for their eventual careers in this exciting field.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: It is too late to attempt to put together a portfolio just before applying for university or polytechnic.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Yet, this is often what many students do, because they go through secondary school with little idea of what they are interested in and do not participate in activities that prepare them for their future careers.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Students from more well-resourced families, on the other hand, often obtain this guidance from their parents and are provided with opportunities for hands-on experience through their parents' professional connections.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: In order to level up our society and capture a wider pool of talent in our population, we need to make this information available to every student.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: However, changing public perceptions and increasing public awareness about health and social care careers takes time and requires a concerted effort from various stakeholders, including the Government, the media, schools and parents.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: We must continue to develop targeted initiatives to address the concerns of healthcare workers, such as work-life balance, remuneration and career progression.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Having said all this, it is simply not sustainable to rely on increasing manpower supply alone to meet the health and social care needs of our nation.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Technology can play an important role in boosting productivity and augmenting manpower.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: In my Adjournment Motion in this House in 2013 on easing the cost of healthcare, I said that technology should be used as a force multiplier in the face of limited manpower in our healthcare system.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This is even more so now than it was a decade ago.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Healthcare technology, or HealthTech, is a fast-growing and promising field which must be developed further in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Transformational technologies are being developed now which will revolutionise the way healthcare is delivered in the future.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: These include AI-driven diagnostics that can detect diseases early and make more accurate diagnoses more quickly than conventional means.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: For example, researchers at Massachusetts Institute of Technology have developed an AI model called Sybil that can predict a patient's risk of lung cancer within six years using low-dose computed tomography scans.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The emerging field of precision medicine has the potential to transform healthcare and is being used in the treatment of diseases like cancer, cardiovascular diseases and genetic disorders.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: It can potentially improve patient outcomes by providing more targeted and effective treatments, reducing adverse reactions to medications and optimising disease prevention strategies.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I note that there is now a Singapore Precision Medicine initiative aiming to generate precision medicine data of up to one million individuals, integrating genomic, lifestyle, health, social and environmental data.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: There are also other healthcare technologies that are not as "deep tech" as what I mentioned earlier but are already in the market and can provide a boost to the productivity of healthcare workers, enhance the patient experience and improve health outcomes.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The National Electronic Health Records (NEHR) system is a major, multi-year HealthTech initiative.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: According to the MOH website, there are 2,231 healthcare institutions participating in the NEHR as of 5 May 2023.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This list appears to be growing every day and I note there has been a marked increase in the number of participating healthcare providers since the start of this year.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The Straits Times reported on 2 May that, "The private sector has been slow to participate in the NEHR since it was launched in 2011".

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: A 2020 survey and paper by Clinical Asst Prof See Qing Yong of Changi General Hospital entitled "Attitudes and Perceptions of General Practitioners Towards the NEHR in Singapore" found that solo practising GPs who are more than 40 years old and who had practised for more than 15 years were less likely to view and contribute data onto the NEHR.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Doctors who regarded themselves as less computer savvy and those who perceived that an inadequate level of technical or financial support was available were also less likely to use the NEHR.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: However, this was deferred in the wake of the cyberattack and data breach of SingHealth's system in July that year, in order for technical end process enhancements to improve the security posture of the NEHR to be implemented first.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Most of these security enhancements were supposed to be completed by last year, according to Senior Minister of State for Health Janil Puthucheary.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Can I ask the Senior Minister of State if all the security enhancements to the NEHR have now been implemented?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I understand that MOH aims to table the Health Information Bill in the second half of this year.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Is MOH reaching out to doctors to address concerns they might have about the security of the patient data they will be required to contribute to the NEHR?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: How is MOH assisting the remaining GPs and dentists to get onboard the NEHR?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: We need to tap on the knowledge and experience of GPs who have been practising for many years, especially as we move forward into the Healthier SG initiative, which will see GPs playing a key role in promoting healthy lifestyles and promoting preventive healthcare.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Technology can be used to help GPs focus on what they do best.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I note that there is a technology subsidy scheme available to help GPs to implement clinic management systems that are compatible with Healthier SG.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: However, implementing these systems still requires a lot of time and effort on the part of GPs and their clinic assistants – time which they simply do not have if they want to focus on direct patient care.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: MOH should explore the possibility of offering an IT manager as a service to GPs and dental clinics.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This would enable them to benefit from the expertise of IT professionals who can assist them in resolving their healthcare IT-related issues.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I have proposed some ways in my speech on how we can do so and I hope that MOH and MOE will consider them.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: As the world celebrates International Nurses Day this Friday on 12 May, which is the anniversary of Florence Nightingale's birth, I would like to take this opportunity to say a huge thank you to all our nurses in both public and private healthcare institutions in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: We appreciate your selfless service, sacrifice and care for our people.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: PSP, once again, thanks all healthcare workers for their sacrifices and dedication to serving Singaporeans, especially during the past three years of the pandemic.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We welcome the Government's move to support healthcare through the Healthier SG initiative, which shifts away from a transactional system that reactively cares for those who are already sick towards an outcome-based system aimed at preventing Singaporeans from falling ill.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Hon Members Dr Tan Yia Swam, Dr Shahira Abdullah and Mr Abdul Samad have spoken passionately about ground-up improvements involving the doctors, healthcare workers, patients and society at large.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We support those improvements that they had mentioned but we also think that they can be better realised by first looking at how to reform healthcare financing and bringing healthcare costs under control.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: PSP defines sustainability in healthcare as providing the most effective healthcare to all Singaporeans that is affordable and equitable.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The focus should not be on protecting the Government's coffers alone but on how to put in place a healthcare system that has the proper incentives to encourage healthy living and, at the same time, covers Singaporeans for all medical circumstances throughout their lives.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Currently, Singaporeans shoulder much of the cost of healthcare through their MediSave savings, their children's MediSave savings, payments from MediShield Life, private insurance and cash outlay.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I acknowledge that over the past decade, the Government has spent more on healthcare, with the introduction of schemes like the Pioneer and Merdeka Generation Packages as well as CHAS.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But the actual spending of these packages is small, relative to the needs of some Singaporeans of the Pioneer and Merdeka Generations who do not have much MediSave savings.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The actual spending is also small, relative to the total assets of the Pioneer Generation Fund and the Merdeka Generation Fund.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Overall, the Government has not contributed enough to cover healthcare expenditure.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Singaporeans are experiencing first-world healthcare cost but receiving much less first-world financial support from the Government.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Healthcare spending has more than doubled over the past two decades.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is not sustainable for Singaporeans to continue footing much of their healthcare bills as well as those of their parents and children.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: To reduce social inequality, the Government must do more to help Singaporeans cope with rising healthcare costs and strengthen their financial security.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: People do not choose to fall ill, whether they are rich or poor.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But while a wealthier family can handle a medical catastrophe better, a similar catastrophe can easily wipe out the MediSave and cash savings of a low-income family even after MediShield payouts.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As a result, Madam, I would like to make three recommendations to reduce the financial burden of healthcare for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: One, the Government should pay for MediShield and CareShield Life premiums for all Singapore Citizens.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Retirement adequacy for Singaporeans is a perennial issue.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: First, housing cost depletes most of their Central Provident Fund (CPF) savings.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, many Singaporeans must continue to work beyond their retirement age to survive without selling their HDB flats.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Insurance premiums take up another chunk of their CPF savings, which could have been used for retirement.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If the premium increases by 10% every five years, which is highly possible, the financial drain could be more than $250,000.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In other words, if the family did not need to pay MediShield and CareShield premiums, the parents would have more than $250,000 extra CPF savings for retirement at age 65.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This will allow the average Singaporean to have their MediSave balances enjoy the compounding effect of the CPF interest for a longer period and be better prepared for a medical event.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Healthier MediSave balances would ultimately strengthen the retirement adequacy of Singaporeans, because less CPF savings will need to be transferred to their MediSave Account.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: My second recommendation is for the Government to top up and expand the use of MediSave, increase MediFund support for needy Singaporeans and increase Pioneer and Merdeka Generation Fund support for older Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is a tiny percentage and has decreased from 2015, when $905 million, or 1.2%, was withdrawn from a $76 billion balance.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This does not make sense, given Singapore's ageing population and increasing demand for healthcare.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Are the rules of withdrawal from the MediSave Account too restrictive?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Government has always restricted withdrawals from the MediSave Account.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But, on aggregate, Singaporeans are not even fully utilising the interest they earn each year on their MediSave balances for medical expenses, let alone their principal sums.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The withholding of MediSave monies for use by its owner is even more unjustifiable than the requirement to maintain a Minimum Sum balance for the Retirement Account.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I, therefore, repeat my call for the MediSave withdrawal limit to be relaxed.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I also echo my colleague Ms Hazel Poa's suggestion at Budget 2021 for the expansion of MediSave eligibility for outpatient treatment.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For low-income Singaporeans who have below average MediSave balances and, therefore, have trouble paying medical expenses, the Government should provide more help by either topping up their MediSave Account or increasing assistance from the MediFund substantially.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Pioneer and Medeka Generation Fund should also increase its payout to help older Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: My third recommendation is for the Government to centralise drug procurement across public and private medical institutions.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Currently, drug procurement is centralised for Singapore's three public healthcare clusters but not for private medical institutions.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Consequently, private clinics generally pay more for drugs than the public sector, which can negotiate good prices.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This drives up costs across the healthcare chain.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Insurance must charge higher premiums to cover higher drug prices.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This will cause the national healthcare expenditure to rise unsustainably.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This will reduce our overall cost of drugs by maximising our bargaining power as a small nation with the big pharmaceutical companies.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In the public sector, the Government should ensure that the price of drugs charged to all Singaporean patients, subsidised or non-subsidised, is at or near the cost price of drugs.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Government can provide additional subsidies to lower drug costs for subsidised patients.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But drug prices should not be marked up unreasonably for non-subsidised patients to cross-subsidise the subsidised patients.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is reasonable to charge non-subsidised patients higher prices for the better services that they receive, but not the drugs they take because they are the same.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: A centralised drug procurement system at the national level would do away with the need for sudden policy changes to control healthcare costs, provide certainty to Singaporeans and strengthen their retirement adequacy.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This can amplify the benefits brought about by initiatives, such as Healthier SG.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For many Singaporeans, financial pressures from the high cost of living are a major cause of their poor health, including the growing problem of mental illnesses.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If more is done to improve the affordability and equity of Singapore's healthcare system, we can expect an improvement in the general health of Singaporeans as well.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This should be one of the national priorities as we support healthcare beyond the COVID-19 pandemic.
